judgments.title: Yes Bank Ltd v. Axis Trustee Services Ltd
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal No. 3182 of 2025 and connected appeals
judgments.bench: Dipankar Datta and Augustine George Masih JJ.
judgments.issue: Could the Administrator write down the bank's AT-1 bonds after the reconstruction scheme had come into force without a write-down clause?
holding: No. The appeals were dismissed and the write-down stays quashed. The validity of the decision is judged as on the date it was taken; later events cannot rescue it.

Under the Basel III Master Circular, a write-down at the point of non-viability has to happen before the bank is reconstituted, that is, before the scheme takes effect. Once the final scheme was in force without a write-down clause, the bonds could not be written down contrary to it.
At the point of non-viability it is the Reserve Bank that decides whether instruments are written down, not the bank or its Administrator. The Administrator only stands in place of the board.
The annual coupon remains payable in terms of the information memoranda.
The Court was critical of the sale of these high-risk instruments to individual investors, which the Master Circular did not permit.
impact: Loss-absorption terms in regulatory capital instruments will be enforced, but only if the regulator and the issuer follow the sequence and the decision-maker laid down in the Reserve Bank's capital framework and in the scheme itself.

Issuers and distributors of AT-1 and similar instruments (banks, and NBFCs issuing perpetual debt) should keep to the permitted investor classes and give clear risk disclosure. Mis-selling to retail investors was a central concern.
statutes: RBI Master Circular - Basel III Capital Regulations, Annex 16
judgments.status_note: The bank and the Reserve Bank filed review petitions in November 2026, which are pending. The ruling affirms the Bombay High Court's judgment of 20 January 2023 in Writ Petition No. 785 of 2021.
judgments.facts: A private sector bank issued Additional Tier 1 bonds of Rs 3,000 crore in 2016 and Rs 5,415 crore in 2017. On 5 March 2020 the bank was placed under moratorium and an Administrator was appointed. The draft reconstruction scheme published next day provided for the bonds to be written down, but the final scheme notified on 13 March 2020 did not. On 14 March 2020 the Administrator wrote the bonds down in full. The Bombay High Court quashed the write-down in January 2023, and the bank, the Reserve Bank and the Union appealed.

judgments.title: Shikha Ghosh v. Axis Bank Ltd
judgments.bench: Prathiba M. Singh and Dinesh Bhatt JJ.
judgments.topic: Bank's mass use of one arbitrator
judgments.issue: Is an award by an arbitrator appointed unilaterally by the lender enforceable, and what should regulators do about the practice?
holding: The bank conceded that awards by arbitrators it had appointed alone are void, following Perkins Eastman and CORE (2025). The award was declared unenforceable against the borrower, and the bank was left free to take fresh recovery steps in accordance with law.

The same arbitrator had handled 4,155 of the bank's cases. The bank was directed to explain this on affidavit and to say how it would deal with such awards, and RBI was asked to caution banks and consider guidance.
impact: Awards from arbitrators appointed by the lender alone, or used in bulk by one lender, are open to challenge as void, and the court has drawn RBI into the issue. Under section 12(5), an ineligible arbitrator can act only if the parties waive the bar by express written agreement after the dispute has arisen.

judgments.status_note: The court kept the matter part-heard for affidavits from the bank and RBI, so further orders may follow.
judgments.facts: A borrower challenged an award passed by a sole arbitrator whom the bank had appointed alone under the loan agreement. It emerged that the same arbitrator had been given thousands of the bank's recovery cases.

judgments.title: Bhadra International (India) Pvt Ltd v. Airports Authority of India
judgments.bench: J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan JJ.
judgments.issue: Is an award by a sole arbitrator appointed by one party alone valid, and can the other party lose its objection by taking part in the arbitration?
holding: The unilateral appointment of a sole arbitrator is void from the start, and the arbitrator is ineligible under section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule. Where the arbitration agreement itself breaches section 12(5), no appointment made under it is valid.
Ineligibility can be waived only by an express agreement in writing after disputes arise. It cannot be waived by implication or conduct.
An arbitrator who is ineligible lacks inherent jurisdiction, so the objection can be raised at any stage, including for the first time in a challenge to the award under section 34.
impact: Recovery awards obtained through a sole arbitrator named by the lender alone can be set aside even if the borrower took part without objecting. Lenders should obtain a clear written waiver after the dispute arises, or have the arbitrator appointed jointly, by an institution or by the court.
Lenders and brokers should review loan agreements, client agreements and pending arbitrations for unilateral appointment clauses.
statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 14, 18, 34 and Seventh Schedule

judgments.title: PNB Housing Finance Ltd v. Manoj Saha
judgments.bench: P.S. Narasimha and Joymalya Bagchi JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a person claiming an old, unregistered tenancy get back possession of a mortgaged property that a housing finance company has taken under SARFAESI?
holding: A person claiming tenancy through an oral or unregistered agreement must prove it with independent evidence such as rent receipts, tax receipts or electricity bills for the period before the demand notice under section 13(2).
Even if proved, such a tenancy does not continue beyond one year from the section 13(2) notice; after that the occupant is a tenant at sufferance.
A recital in the sale deed or a letter of attornment from the borrower is not enough. The High Court's order restoring possession was set aside.
impact: Lenders can resist tenancy claims set up to block possession of mortgaged homes, by insisting on proof of occupation before the demand notice.
At loan origination, HFCs should record who occupies the property and on what terms.

judgments.title: Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Ltd v. 63 Moons Technologies Ltd
judgments.bench: Bela M. Trivedi and Satish Chandra Sharma JJ.
judgments.topic: Resolution of a housing finance company under the IBC
judgments.issue: Could the appellate tribunal reopen the plan's treatment of section 66 recoveries, are deposit holders entitled to full repayment, and can directors of a superseded board take part in the committee of creditors?
holding: The plan was restored. How recoveries are dealt with is a commercial decision of the committee of creditors, and the NCLAT could not substitute its own view.

Avoidance applications (preferential, undervalued and extortionate transactions) are different from fraudulent and wrongful trading applications under section 66. The plan could assign section 66 recoveries to the resolution applicant, while the NCLT still decides those applications.
A vote cast by the authorised representative for a class of creditors binds every member of that class, including those who voted against.
Fixed deposit holders cannot claim full repayment by relying on section 45QA of the RBI Act or section 36A of the National Housing Bank Act. Once the plan is approved, they are bound by it.
Directors of a board superseded by the Reserve Bank under section 45-IE are not 'suspended directors'. They cannot attend committee meetings or demand copies of the plan.
impact: For lenders and bidders, the ruling confirms that the special route for NBFCs and HFCs works like an ordinary insolvency once it starts, with the Reserve Bank's administrator in charge and the old board out.
Depositors and debenture holders of a failed NBFC or HFC are creditors under the plan and take what the plan gives their class.
statutes: Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, ss. 45-IE, 45QA

links.label: NBFCs of Rs 500 crore notified as FSPs

judgments.status_note: From 26 May 2026 the substituted section 26 expressly provides that avoidance and fraudulent or wrongful trading applications do not affect the insolvency process and continue after it ends.
judgments.facts: The Reserve Bank superseded the board of a large housing finance company and, as the first use of the special insolvency route for financial service providers, started its corporate insolvency. The approved resolution plan gave the benefit of any recoveries from fraudulent trading applications (section 66) to the resolution applicant, valuing them at a notional Re 1. A debenture holder objected, and the NCLAT sent that term back to the creditors. Fixed deposit holders demanded full repayment, and former promoters and directors sought to take part in the process.

judgments.title: Mahaveer Sharma v. Exide Life Insurance Co. Ltd
judgments.bench: B.V. Nagarathna and S.C. Sharma JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a life insurer reject a claim because the insured disclosed one large existing policy but not some smaller ones?
holding: No. The insured had disclosed a Rs 40 lakh policy, much larger than the undisclosed policies and the policy in question. That was a substantial disclosure.
The undisclosed policies were of inconsequential amounts, and their omission was not a material suppression. The repudiation was set aside.
impact: Not every omission is material. Insurers should ask whether the missing fact would have changed a prudent insurer's decision before repudiating.

judgments.title: Home Kraft Avenues v. Jayesh Sanghrajka (Resolution Professional, Ornate Spaces Pvt Ltd)
judgments.bench: Yogesh Khanna J. and Arun Baroka
judgments.issue: Does failure to register a charge stop a creditor being treated as secured in the CIRP?
holding: No. In the CIRP, a security interest can be proved by other evidence; non-registration under section 77 does not by itself stop the creditor being a secured creditor.
impact: The position differs in liquidation, where registration or other proof under the Liquidation Regulations is needed (Volkswagen Finance, 2020). Registration remains the safe course.
judgments.facts: In a company's insolvency a creditor's security interest had not been registered with the Registrar of Companies under section 77. The question was whether it could be classified as a secured creditor in the resolution process.

judgments.title: AC Chokshi Share Broker Pvt Ltd v. Jatin Pratap Desai
judgments.bench: P.S. Narasimha and Sandeep Mehta JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a broker invoke exchange arbitration against a husband for his wife's trading debt, based on an oral arrangement?
holding: Yes. Courts must read contracts practically, looking at the parties' conduct and intention. The husband's oral instructions and the joint way the two accounts were operated showed joint and several liability.
Separate client registration agreements, client codes and accounts did not change this. Arbitration under the exchange bye-laws was maintainable against the husband.
impact: Brokers who act on a client's oral instructions to move credit balances to a family member's account may be able to recover from both. This does not relax SEBI's requirements on evidence of client orders, which still apply.

judgments.title: State Bank of India v. IDBI Bank Ltd
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan J. (Chairperson) and Barun Mitra
judgments.topic: Liquidation proceeds shared by admitted claims
judgments.issue: How are liquidation proceeds shared among secured creditors who relinquished their security?
holding: In proportion to admitted claims, following the Supreme Court in India Resurgence ARC v. Amit Metaliks (2021), subject to the outcome of the pending Supreme Court appeal against the Technology Development Board ruling.
impact: Until the Supreme Court decides, liquidators distribute pro rata to admitted claims among secured creditors in the same class.
judgments.status_note: Subject to the Supreme Court's decision on the Technology Development Board appeal.
judgments.facts: Secured lenders in a liquidation disagreed on how the sale proceeds should be shared: by the value of each lender's security or in proportion to admitted claims.

judgments.title: Assistant Commissioner, CGST and Central Excise v. Pradeep Kabra (Cengres Tiles Ltd)
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan J. (Chairperson), Barun Mitra and Arun Baroka
judgments.topic: Excise and GST dues in a resolution plan
judgments.issue: Are central excise and GST dues secured debt, entitling the department to more than the plan offered?
holding: No. These dues are operational debts. Rainbow Papers turned on the statutory first charge under the Gujarat VAT Act and did not apply. The appeal was dismissed.
impact: Central tax departments rank as operational creditors. After the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, government dues have a fixed place in section 53 regardless of any statutory charge.
statutes: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
judgments.facts: The tax department's admitted claim of about Rs 11.77 crore for excise and GST dues was given Rs 1 lakh under the approved resolution plan. It appealed, relying on Rainbow Papers to argue it was a secured creditor.

judgments.title: Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp. Ltd v. Awaz
judgments.bench: Bela M. Trivedi and Satish Chandra Sharma JJ.
judgments.issue: Could the National Consumer Commission cap credit card interest at 30% a year as an unfair trade practice?
holding: The National Commission's ruling that interest above 30% a year is usurious was set aside. It was contrary to section 21A of the Banking Regulation Act, which bars courts and tribunals from reopening a bank transaction on the ground that the interest is excessive, and it encroached on RBI's domain.
Directions and guidelines issued by RBI are an extension of the statute. Interest charged as RBI's circulars allow is not an unfair trade practice in itself.
The complaint was not maintainable: the trusts that filed it were not 'persons' or consumers, and no permission to sue in a representative capacity had been obtained.
impact: Interest on credit cards and loans is set by the lender's Board-approved policy within RBI's framework, not by consumer forums. Transparency rules (KFS, APR and disclosure of charges) still apply.
The bar in section 21A is written for banking companies, so NBFCs should rely on the RBI framework and fair-dealing rules rather than on section 21A itself.

judgments.title: EIH Ltd v. Subodh Kumar Agrawal (Golden Jubilee Hotels)
judgments.bench: Rakesh Kumar Jain J. and Naresh Salecha
judgments.issue: Can a resolution plan terminate the corporate debtor's existing contracts, and how far can the tribunals review the committee's decision?
holding: Yes. The committee's commercial decision to approve a plan that ends existing contracts cannot be questioned, provided the plan complies with section 30(2).
Judicial review is limited to the grounds in sections 30(2), 31 and 61(3).
impact: Counterparties of a borrower in insolvency, such as operators and service providers, may see their contracts ended by the plan.
judgments.facts: A hotel operator had a management contract with a hotel company that went into insolvency. The approved resolution plan terminated the contract, and the operator challenged the plan.

judgments.title: Hare Ram Singh v. Reserve Bank of India
judgments.bench: Dharmesh Sharma J.
judgments.issue: Who bears the loss from a phishing or vishing fraud that the customer reports promptly?
holding: Under the Reserve Bank's 2017 circular on customer protection in unauthorised electronic banking transactions, the burden of proving the customer's liability is on the bank.

Clicking a fraudulent link is not by itself gross negligence. The bank did not show that the customer gave away his credentials, did not act promptly to block or recall the money, and its controls for authenticating the transactions fell short of the Reserve Bank's digital payment security requirements.
The customer had zero liability. The bank was directed to refund Rs 2.60 lakh with interest at 9 per cent a year and pay Rs 25,000 in costs.
impact: Banks, card issuers and prepaid instrument issuers should record the evidence of customer negligence at the time, act on a fraud report immediately (blocking, chargeback or recall) and be able to show that authentication worked. Without that, the loss stays with the institution.
statutes: RBI circular on Customer Protection - Limiting Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions, 6 July 2017
RBI Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls, 2021
judgments.facts: A bank customer clicked a link in a message that appeared to come from his bank, and Rs 2.60 lakh was debited from his account in April 2021. He reported it at once to the bank and the police. The bank said he had shared his credentials and refused a refund. The Banking Ombudsman directed payment of only a part of the amount.

judgments.title: Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v. ECI SPIC SMO MCML (JV)
judgments.bench: Five Judges, D.Y. Chandrachud CJI presiding
judgments.issue: Is a clause valid if it lets one party appoint a sole arbitrator, or makes the other side choose from a panel curated by that party?
holding: Equal treatment of parties applies at every stage of arbitration, including the appointment of arbitrators.

A clause that lets one party unilaterally appoint a sole arbitrator gives rise to justifiable doubts about the arbitrator's independence and impartiality, and hinders the other party's equal participation. For a three-member tribunal, forcing the other party to pick its arbitrator from a panel curated by one side breaches equal treatment.

A party can still expressly waive the objection in writing after disputes arise (proviso to section 12(5)). The Court said the law it laid down applies prospectively to appointments made after 8 November 2024, and that this direction applies to three-member tribunals.
impact: Loan agreements that let the lender alone name the arbitrator are unsafe. Lenders should agree on the arbitrator with the borrower, use an arbitral institution, or apply to the court under section 11.

Awards by an arbitrator the lender appointed alone, without an express written waiver by the borrower after the dispute arose, are at risk of being set aside. Bhadra International (2026) confirms that such a sole arbitrator is ineligible.

links.label: Responsible Business Conduct (Fair Practices, KFS, penal charges, recovery)

judgments.status_note: Prospective for appointments after 8 November 2024, as stated for three-member tribunals.

judgments.title: State Bank of India v. Pallabh Bhowmick
judgments.bench: Lanusungkum Jamir and Kardak Ete JJ.
judgments.topic: Unauthorised electronic transactions: proof of negligence
judgments.issue: Is a customer who is tricked into installing an application negligent, so that the bank need not refund the loss?
holding: The Division Bench upheld the direction to refund. The bank has to prove the customer's negligence with cogent material; a general allegation that he must have shared credentials is not enough.
The loss arose from a third-party breach and was reported within the time allowed by the Reserve Bank's 2017 circular, so the customer's liability was zero. The bank had also not raised a chargeback.
impact: Read with the Delhi High Court's ruling in Hare Ram Singh, the position is that prompt reporting shifts the loss to the bank unless it can prove the customer's negligence. An Ombudsman closure does not prevent the High Court from granting relief.
statutes: RBI circular on Customer Protection - Limiting Liability of Customers in Unauthorised Electronic Banking Transactions, 6 July 2017
judgments.status_note: The Supreme Court dismissed the bank's special leave petition on 3 January 2025.
judgments.facts: After a data breach at an online retailer, a fraudster posing as its customer care persuaded a customer to install a mobile application. Rs 94,204.80 was then taken from his bank account in October 2021. He reported it within a day. The bank refused a refund, alleging that he must have shared his one-time passwords, and the Banking Ombudsman closed his complaint. A single judge directed the bank to refund the amount.

judgments.title: BRS Ventures Investments Ltd v. SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd
judgments.bench: Abhay S. Oka and Pankaj Mithal JJ.
judgments.topic: Recovering from both borrower and corporate guarantor
judgments.issue: After receiving part payment in the corporate guarantor's insolvency, can the lender proceed against the principal borrower for the balance?
holding: Yes. Part payment under the guarantor's resolution plan does not extinguish the borrower's liability for the rest. The liability of borrower and surety is co-extensive, and the creditor can proceed against both, together or one after the other.
A holding company does not own the assets of its subsidiary. The subsidiary's assets cannot be treated as part of the holding company's resolution plan.
The guarantor (or whoever steps into its shoes) is subrogated to the creditor's rights only to the extent of the amount actually paid.
impact: Lenders can file separate or simultaneous section 7 applications against the borrower and the corporate guarantor, and accepting a payout in one does not close the claim in the other, so long as total recovery does not exceed the debt.
Buyers of a guarantor company under a plan get subrogation rights only for what was paid, not control over the borrower's assets.
judgments.facts: An NBFC lent Rs 100 crore to a company, with the borrower's holding company as corporate guarantor. In the guarantor's insolvency the NBFC received Rs 38.87 crore under the resolution plan. It then filed for insolvency of the borrower for the balance. The successful resolution applicant of the guarantor argued that the debt stood satisfied and that the borrower's assets were part of the guarantor's plan.

judgments.title: Mahakali Sujatha v. Branch Manager, Future Generali India Life Insurance Co. Ltd
judgments.bench: B.V. Nagarathna and Augustine George Masih JJ.
judgments.issue: Who must prove that the insured suppressed other policies, and with what evidence?
holding: Where the insurer repudiates on the ground of suppression, the burden is on the insurer to prove that the fact suppressed was material and that the insured knew of it.
The insurer had produced no documents to show the other policies. The repudiation could not stand.
impact: Claims teams must keep documentary proof, such as other insurers' records, before repudiating for non-disclosure. Allegations alone will fail.

judgments.title: Milind Patel v. Union Bank of India
judgments.bench: B.P. Colabawalla and Somasekhar Sundaresan JJ.
judgments.topic: Wilful defaulter process: disclosure and reasons
judgments.issue: What must a lender disclose and record when it declares a person a wilful defaulter?
holding: The lender must give the person all the material relevant to the proposed declaration, not only what it relies on. That includes material that helps the person's case.

Both the identification committee and the review committee must pass reasoned orders, and those orders must be served on the person. The members of the committees who took the decision should be identifiable.
The bank withdrew its orders, and the Court directed the credit information companies to remove the petitioner's name.
impact: Lenders (banks and NBFCs to whom the wilful defaulter directions apply) should send the full record with the show cause notice, record reasons at both stages and keep the committee composition on file. Orders passed on a bare notice are likely to be set aside.
A wilful defaulter tag closes access to credit and has reputational effects, so courts hold lenders to a strict standard of fairness.
statutes: RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 1 July 2015 (since replaced by the 2024 Directions)

links.label: Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters

judgments.facts: A former joint managing director of an infrastructure finance group received a show cause notice from a bank proposing to declare him a wilful defaulter for the group's borrowings. The notice did not enclose the material relied on, and the orders of the bank's identification and review committees gave no real reasons.

judgments.title: Shakti Yezdani v. Jayanand Jayant Salgaonkar
judgments.bench: Hrishikesh Roy and Pankaj Mithal JJ.
judgments.issue: Does a nominee of shares or securities become the owner on the holder's death, to the exclusion of the legal heirs?
holding: No. The nominee does not get absolute title. Vesting in the nominee under section 109A of the Companies Act, 1956 (section 72 of the 2013 Act) and Bye-law 9.11.1 under the Depositories Act is for a limited purpose.
Nomination does not change the law of succession. The legal heirs, or the beneficiaries under a will, remain entitled.
impact: Depository participants, brokers and registrars can transmit securities to the nominee to complete formalities, but the nominee holds them subject to the claims of the legal heirs.
Client communication should say clearly that a nomination is not a will.

judgments.title: Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud CJI, J.B. Pardiwala and Manoj Misra JJ.
judgments.issue: Are sections 95 to 100 of the IBC, on insolvency of individuals such as personal guarantors, constitutional?
holding: Sections 95 to 100 are valid and do not violate Articles 14 and 21.
The resolution professional only facilitates and recommends. No adjudication happens until the Adjudicating Authority decides under section 100, and natural justice must be observed at that stage.

No hearing is needed before the resolution professional is appointed under section 97(5). The debtor can take part when the resolution professional examines the application under section 99. The interim moratorium under section 96 stays legal proceedings in respect of any debt.
impact: Lenders can file insolvency against personal guarantors of corporate borrowers without a prior hearing on 'jurisdictional facts'. The guarantor is heard in the resolution professional's examination and before the Adjudicating Authority decides.
judgments.status_note: From 26-05-2026, s. 96(4), inserted by the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, provides that the interim moratorium does not apply to personal guarantors to corporate debtors. The rest of the ruling is unaffected.

judgments.title: IFCI Ltd v. Sutanu Sinha
judgments.bench: Sanjay Kishan Kaul, Sudhanshu Dhulia and Ahsanuddin Amanullah JJ.
judgments.issue: Are compulsorily convertible debentures debt or equity for a claim in insolvency?
holding: The CCDs were equity. The project documents treated them as equity, they were never recategorised with the concessioning authority's approval, and repayment obligations lay with the sponsor, not the company.
Instruments compulsorily convertible into shares are generally equity, not debt. The holder was not a financial creditor.
impact: On these project documents, CCD holders ranked as shareholders. Whether an instrument is debt or equity turns on its terms and how the parties treated it; a redemption obligation points towards debt.

links.label: Master Direction – Foreign Investment in India

judgments.facts: IFCI had subscribed to compulsorily convertible debentures (CCDs) of a toll-road project company. In the company's insolvency it claimed as a financial creditor; the resolution professional rejected the claim because the project documents, the concessioning authority and the lenders had treated the CCDs as equity.

judgments.title: Celir LLP v. Bafna Motors (Mumbai) Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud CJI and J.B. Pardiwala J.
judgments.issue: Until when can a borrower redeem a mortgaged property that a secured creditor is selling under SARFAESI?
holding: Under section 13(8) of SARFAESI as amended in 2016, the borrower's right to redeem ends on the date the auction notice is published under Rule 9(1) of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, not when the sale is completed.
SARFAESI, as a special law with an overriding clause, prevails over the general right of redemption in section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act.

Once the sale is confirmed, the lender cannot withhold the sale certificate and make a private settlement with the borrower. High Courts should not use writ jurisdiction to undo an auction when the remedy under section 17 is available.
impact: Borrowers must pay in full before the auction notice is published. After that, lenders should complete the sale and should not accept late settlements that defeat the auction purchaser.
Auction purchasers get firmer title, which supports bids at SARFAESI auctions.

judgments.title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd v. Anuj Jain (Resolution Professional, Ballarpur Industries Ltd)
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan J. (Chairperson) and Naresh Salecha
judgments.topic: Resolution plan can extinguish third-party security
judgments.issue: Can a resolution plan extinguish security that the corporate debtor gave for a third party's loan?
holding: Yes. The plan can extinguish such security interests; the lender's consent is not required.
The lender keeps its claim against the principal borrower and can ask that borrower for fresh security.
impact: Third-party security from a company that goes into insolvency can be lost under its plan. Lenders should monitor group companies' insolvencies and take guarantees.
judgments.facts: An asset reconstruction company held loans given to a group company that were secured by assets of the corporate debtor. The resolution plan for the corporate debtor released that security without the lender's consent.

judgments.title: Vistra ITCL (India) Ltd v. Dinkar Venkatasubramanian
judgments.bench: M.R. Shah and Sanjiv Khanna JJ.
judgments.topic: Pledgee for a third party's loan in a resolution plan
judgments.issue: What rights does a lender holding only a pledge from the corporate debtor for someone else's loan have in the debtor's insolvency?
holding: The pledgee is not a financial creditor of the pledgor (following Anuj Jain and Phoenix ARC), so it has no seat or vote on the committee of creditors.

It is a secured creditor and keeps the rights of a secured creditor under sections 52 and 53 and the pledge agreement. It cannot be treated worse than a dissenting financial creditor or an operational creditor.
impact: Third-party security holders keep their rights as secured creditors and can object to a plan that ignores their security. The Court noted that giving them a vote to the value of the security would need a larger bench to revisit Anuj Jain and Phoenix ARC.
judgments.facts: Amtek Auto had pledged shares it held to a security trustee, Vistra, to secure loans to a group company. In Amtek's insolvency, Vistra was not treated as a financial creditor and the resolution plan did not deal properly with its pledge.

judgments.title: South Indian Bank Ltd v. Naveen Mathew Philip
judgments.bench: Sanjiv Khanna and M.M. Sundresh JJ.
judgments.issue: Should High Courts entertain writ petitions against SARFAESI notices when the Debts Recovery Tribunal is available?
holding: The power under Article 226 is wide but should be used only in extraordinary cases. Where the legislature has provided a specific remedy, as SARFAESI does through the Debts Recovery Tribunal, the writ remedy should not be used.
A writ of mandamus in a commercial matter against a private party needs a clear legal right, and more caution is needed when the respondent is a private lender.
impact: Borrowers challenging SARFAESI measures will normally be sent to the DRT under section 17. This reduces stays obtained through writ petitions.

judgments.title: State Bank of India v. Rajesh Agarwal
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud CJI and Hima Kohli J.
judgments.issue: Must a lender hear the borrower before classifying its account as fraud under RBI's Master Directions on Frauds?
holding: Classifying an account as fraud has civil consequences for the borrower: the penal measures that apply to wilful defaulters, no restructuring and, in effect, a credit freeze that the Court described as close to 'civil death'.

The Master Directions do not expressly exclude a hearing, so the rule of audi alteram partem is read into them. The borrower must be given notice, a chance to explain the forensic audit findings and to make a representation before the account is classified as fraud.
The decision classifying the account as fraud must be made by a reasoned order.
impact: Every fraud classification needs a show-cause notice with the material relied on, a real chance to reply in writing, and a reasoned order. Classifications made without these are open to challenge in writ proceedings.

In State Bank of India v. Amit Iron Pvt Ltd (7 April 2026, 2026 INSC 323) the Supreme Court held that the borrower has no right to a personal hearing, and that forensic audit reports the lender relies on should be furnished to the borrower. A lender that wants to withhold a report to protect third parties must first show that disclosure would affect their rights.
RBI's Fraud Risk Management Directions for NBFCs now build these steps into the process.

links.label: Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters

judgments.status_note: Clarified in State Bank of India v. Amit Iron Pvt Ltd (2026 INSC 323): no personal hearing is needed, and the steps it requires are part of RBI's Master Directions of 2024 on fraud.

judgments.title: Shapoorji Pallonji and Co. Pvt Ltd v. Korba West Power Company Ltd
judgments.bench: Anant Bijay Singh J. and Shreesha Merla
judgments.topic: Arbitration claims in a resolution plan
judgments.issue: What happens to an operational creditor's claims pending in arbitration when a resolution plan is approved?
holding: The plan was upheld. The contractor, whose claim had been treated as contingent, was given liberty to continue the arbitration and have its claim decided.
On the resolution applicant's appeal (Civil Appeal No. 1741 of 2023), the Supreme Court held that any award could not add to the applicant's obligations beyond the approved plan.
impact: Claims not provided for in an approved plan are extinguished (Ghanashyam Mishra, 2021). A pending arbitration may at most quantify a claim; it cannot impose a new liability on the resolution applicant.
judgments.facts: A contractor had claims against a company in insolvency that were pending in arbitration. The resolution plan did not deal with them, and the contractor appealed against the plan's approval.

judgments.title: Wave Megacity Centre Pvt Ltd v. Rakesh Taneja
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan J. (Chairperson) and Barun Mitra
judgments.issue: Can a company's own insolvency application be rejected as filed with fraudulent or malicious intent?
holding: Yes. The application was rejected under section 65 as filed to defeat a creditor rather than to resolve insolvency.
The section 10A bar on filings for defaults during the COVID-19 period does not cover defaults before 25 March 2020.
impact: Lenders and authorities can resist a borrower's tactical self-filing by showing malicious intent.

links.label: Due diligence on misuse of the IBC

judgments.facts: A real estate developer filed for its own insolvency under section 10, largely to avoid dues to the development authority. The authority argued the filing was fraudulent.

judgments.title: Maitreya Doshi v. Anand Rathi Global Finance Ltd
judgments.bench: Indira Banerjee and J.K. Maheshwari JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a financial creditor start insolvency against two companies that are both liable for the same debt?
holding: Yes. If both companies are corporate debtors for the same debt, section 7 proceedings may be brought against both. A pledgor as such may not be a financial debtor, but Doshi Holdings had been found to be a co-borrower.
The creditor cannot recover the same amount twice. What it recovers from one reduces what it can claim from the other.
impact: Lenders can run parallel insolvencies against a borrower and a co-borrower or corporate guarantor, and must give credit in each for recoveries made in the other.
judgments.facts: An NBFC lent to Premier Ltd under loan-cum-pledge agreements that Doshi Holdings signed both as a borrower and as a pledgor of shares. After Premier's insolvency began, the NBFC filed a section 7 application against Doshi Holdings too.

judgments.title: Small Industries Development Bank of India v. Vivek Raheja (Resolution Professional, Gupta Exim (India) Pvt Ltd)
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan J. (Chairperson) and Barun Mitra
judgments.topic: Distribution under a resolution plan by voting share
judgments.issue: Must a resolution plan distribute proceeds according to the value of each creditor's security?
holding: No. The committee of creditors may distribute by voting share. A dissenting secured creditor is entitled only to what it would get in liquidation under section 53, not to the value of its security.
impact: Lenders holding better security should negotiate within the committee; the value of their collateral is not guaranteed in a resolution plan.
judgments.status_note: In DBS Bank v. Ruchi Soya (2024 INSC 14) the Supreme Court referred to a larger bench what a dissenting secured financial creditor must receive under a plan.
judgments.facts: A secured lender with a charge on particular assets objected that the resolution plan distributed proceeds by voting share rather than by the value of each lender's security.

judgments.title: State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Ltd
judgments.bench: Indira Banerjee and A.S. Bopanna JJ.
judgments.topic: State tax dues as secured debt
judgments.issue: Is a State with a statutory first charge for tax dues a secured creditor under the IBC, and can a plan ignore those dues?
holding: A charge created by statute is a 'security interest', so the State was a secured creditor and its dues ranked with secured creditors in the section 53 waterfall.
A resolution plan that does not provide for statutory dues as required is not binding and can be rejected.
impact: For a time this put tax authorities alongside secured lenders. The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, in force from 26 May 2026, now places government dues at their own place in section 53 whether or not a security interest arises by operation of law, which removes that parity.
statutes: Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003, s. 48
judgments.status_note: The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 ranks government dues in section 53 regardless of a statutory charge.
judgments.facts: The Gujarat sales tax department claimed VAT dues in the insolvency of Rainbow Papers. Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act gives the State a first charge on the dealer's property. The resolution plan gave the department almost nothing.

judgments.title: Franklin Templeton Trustee Services Pvt Ltd v. Amruta Garg (August 2022)
judgments.case_no: I.A. No. 53453 of 2022 in Civil Appeal Nos. 498-501 of 2021
judgments.bench: S. Abdul Nazeer and Sanjiv Khanna JJ.
judgments.issue: Are mutual fund distributors entitled to trail commission from a scheme that is being wound up?
holding: Regulation 52, which allows recurring expenses including distributor commission, applies only while a scheme is operating, not after the notice of winding up is published.
Distributor commission is not an expense connected with winding up. Future trail commission is not an amount 'due and payable' at the time of winding up.
impact: Once a winding-up notice is published, distributors stop earning trail commission from that scheme. The SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 now say expressly that distribution commission is not a winding-up cost (regulation 38(1)(d), Explanation).
judgments.status_note: Decided under the 1996 Regulations, which the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced from 1 April 2026. The 2026 Regulations follow this ruling.

judgments.title: Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd v. Axis Bank Ltd
judgments.bench: Indira Banerjee and J.K. Maheshwari JJ.
judgments.topic: Must the NCLT admit a lender's insolvency application?
judgments.issue: Is admission of a financial creditor's application under section 7(5)(a) mandatory once a debt and default are shown?
holding: The Court read the word 'may' in section 7(5)(a), in contrast to 'shall' in section 9(5)(a), as giving the NCLT a discretion. It could consider relevant factors such as the overall financial health and viability of the corporate debtor before admitting.

In a later order on a review petition the Court said these observations were made on the facts of the case. In M. Suresh Kumar Reddy v. Canara Bank (2023 INSC 521) the Court held that Vidarbha was confined to its facts and that, once default is shown, admission must ordinarily follow.
impact: For applications decided under the amended section 7(5), the borrower can no longer rely on Vidarbha to resist admission on grounds such as pending claims or general viability. The ruling remains relevant to older matters and to understanding why the provision was rewritten.
judgments.status_note: Section 7(5) was substituted with effect from 26 May 2026: the NCLT shall admit the application within 14 days if a default has occurred, the application is complete and no disciplinary proceeding is pending against the proposed resolution professional, and no other ground may be used to reject it.
judgments.facts: A power generating company defaulted on bank loans. It asked the NCLT to defer the bank's section 7 application because it held an order of the electricity appellate tribunal in its favour worth about Rs 1,730 crore, more than the bank's claim, which was under appeal. The NCLT and NCLAT held that once debt and default are shown, nothing else is relevant.

judgments.title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd v. A. Balakrishnan
judgments.bench: L. Nageswara Rao and B.R. Gavai JJ.
judgments.topic: Recovery certificates and decrees are financial debt
judgments.issue: Is a liability under a DRT recovery certificate a financial debt, and does the certificate give a fresh starting point for limitation?
holding: A liability under a recovery certificate is a financial debt, and its holder is a financial creditor who may file under section 7.
A recovery certificate gives a fresh cause of action, so a section 7 application filed within three years of the certificate is in time.
impact: Lenders that have won at the DRT can still use the IBC, but should file within three years of the recovery certificate.
statutes: Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993, s. 19(22)
judgments.facts: Kotak Mahindra Bank had obtained a recovery certificate from the Debts Recovery Tribunal for a loan, so the certificate arose from a financial debt. It then filed a section 7 application relying on the certificate. The appellate tribunal held that a recovery certificate holder was not a financial creditor.

judgments.title: Oriental Bank of Commerce v. Anil Anchalia (Liquidator of Bala Techno Industries Ltd)
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan J. (Chairperson) and Shreesha Merla
judgments.topic: Exclusive charge holder in liquidation distribution
judgments.issue: Is a secured creditor that relinquishes an exclusive charge paid from the value of that asset, or pro rata with other secured creditors?
holding: Pro rata. After relinquishment, all secured creditors share in proportion to their claims under section 53. The tribunal relied on the Supreme Court's ruling in India Resurgence ARC v. Amit Metaliks (2021).
impact: A lender with an exclusive charge that wants to keep the benefit of it should consider realising the security itself under section 52 rather than relinquishing it.
judgments.status_note: The related question of inter se priority among secured creditors is pending in the Supreme Court.
judgments.facts: A bank with an exclusive charge over certain assets of a company in liquidation relinquished its security and asked to be paid the full sale value of those assets.

judgments.title: Nedumpilli Finance Co Ltd v. State of Kerala
judgments.bench: Hemant Gupta and V. Ramasubramanian JJ.
judgments.topic: State money-lending laws do not apply to NBFCs
judgments.issue: Do State money-lending laws apply to NBFCs registered under the RBI Act and regulated by the Reserve Bank?
holding: No. Chapter III-B of the RBI Act is a complete code, and the Reserve Bank's control over an NBFC runs 'from the cradle to the grave': registration, capital, deposits, prudential norms, directions and winding up.
The Kerala Money Lenders Act, 1958 and the Gujarat Money Lenders Act, 2011 have no application to NBFCs registered under the RBI Act and regulated by the Reserve Bank.
The Reserve Bank has power to deal with the interest NBFCs charge, through sections 45JA and 45L of the RBI Act.
impact: A registered NBFC does not need a State money-lending licence and is not bound by State caps on interest. Its pricing is governed by the Reserve Bank's directions on interest rates, fair practices and, for microfinance loans, the pricing framework.
The ruling does not cover unregistered lenders, and it does not exempt NBFCs from other State laws such as those on coercive recovery, which need to be checked separately.
statutes: Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, Chapter III-B, ss. 45-IA, 45JA, 45L, 45Q

links.label: Registration, Exemptions and Scale Based Regulation

judgments.facts: NBFCs registered with the Reserve Bank were asked by State authorities in Kerala and Gujarat to take money-lending licences and follow the interest caps in the State money lenders Acts. The Kerala High Court held that the State Act applied to them; the Gujarat High Court held that it did not.

judgments.title: Subhankar Bhowmik v. Union of India
judgments.bench: Indrajit Mahanty CJ.
judgments.topic: Decree holders are not financial creditors
judgments.issue: Must the IBC treat decree holders on a par with financial creditors?
holding: No. Decree holders form a different class from financial creditors, and the classification is reasonable. They have no right to a seat on the committee of creditors. The petition was dismissed.
impact: A decree does not by itself make the holder a financial creditor. A lender's decree or recovery certificate for a financial debt is different: see Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan (2022).
judgments.facts: A decree holder filed a public interest petition arguing that the IBC was discriminatory because decree holders were not given a place on the committee of creditors alongside financial creditors.

judgments.title: Shrikant G. Mantri v. Punjab National Bank
judgments.bench: L. Nageswara Rao and B.R. Gavai JJ.
judgments.issue: Is a person who takes a bank facility for his business a 'consumer' who can file a consumer complaint?
holding: No. A service availed for a commercial purpose is outside the definition of 'consumer'. The test is the dominant purpose of the transaction: whether it is closely linked to profit generation.
The overdraft was taken to expand the broker's business, so the relationship was purely business to business. The exception for self-employed persons earning a livelihood did not apply.
impact: Lenders facing consumer complaints from business borrowers on working capital, overdraft or trade facilities can raise this as a threshold objection. Individuals borrowing for personal needs, or to earn a livelihood by self-employment, remain consumers.
statutes: Consumer Protection Act, 1986, s. 2(1)(d) (now Consumer Protection Act, 2019, s. 2(7))
judgments.facts: A stockbroker took an overdraft facility from a bank against a pledge of shares to run his broking business. After a dispute over the sale of pledged shares and the settlement of the account, he filed a consumer complaint claiming deficiency in service.

judgments.title: Pradeep Kumar v. Post Master General
judgments.bench: L. Nageswara Rao, Sanjiv Khanna and B.R. Gavai JJ.
judgments.topic: Liability for fraud by an employee
judgments.issue: Is a post office or bank liable for the fraud or wrongful act of its employee?
holding: Yes. An employer is liable for the fraud or wrong of its employee committed in the course of employment. Proof of the employee's guilt in a criminal case is not required.

Payment in cash to someone other than the holder, contrary to the rules, was not a valid discharge under the Negotiable Instruments Act. The post office could not claim to be a holder or payer in due course.
The post office and its officers were held jointly and severally liable to pay the maturity value with interest, with Rs 1 lakh as compensation.
impact: Banks, NBFCs and other deposit-takers bear the loss when staff collude in paying out a customer's instrument or deposit to the wrong person. The Court expressly applied the same principle to banks.
Controls over cash payouts, identification of the payee and supervision of agents are the practical defence.
judgments.facts: A couple handed Kisan Vikas Patras with a face value of Rs 32.60 lakh to a post office agent to move them to another post office. The certificates were instead encashed, and Rs 25.54 lakh was paid out in cash through the agent with the involvement of a post office employee. The consumer fora refused relief, treating the agent as the investors' own agent.

judgments.title: Phoenix ARC Pvt Ltd v. Vishwa Bharati Vidya Mandir
judgments.bench: M.R. Shah and B.V. Nagarathna JJ.
judgments.topic: No writ petition against a private lender's SARFAESI action
judgments.issue: Can a borrower challenge a private bank's or ARC's SARFAESI measures by writ petition under Article 226?
holding: A writ petition against a private financial institution or ARC over its proposed action under section 13(4) is not maintainable. Lending and recovery by a private lender is a commercial activity and not a public function.
The borrower's remedy is an application to the Debts Recovery Tribunal under section 17. Filing writ petitions to stall recovery was described as an abuse of process.
impact: Private banks, NBFCs, HFCs and ARCs can ask for early dismissal of writ petitions against SARFAESI steps. Borrowers have to use the section 17 route.

links.label: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.facts: An asset reconstruction company that had acquired a loan gave notice of its intention to take possession of the mortgaged properties under the SARFAESI Act. The borrowers filed writ petitions in the High Court, which ordered status quo on a small deposit although about Rs 117 crore was due, and the order continued for years.

judgments.title: Jacob Punnen v. United India Insurance Co. Ltd
judgments.bench: K.M. Joseph and S. Ravindra Bhat JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a health insurer rely on a new cap on cover that it introduced at renewal without telling the policyholder?
holding: The policyholders were led to believe they were renewing the same policy, while the insurer had introduced caps on certain surgical procedures. The insurer had a duty to tell them about the new limits.
Failing to disclose the changed terms was a deficiency in service. The District Forum's order allowing the claim was restored.
impact: Any change to cover at renewal, particularly limits and sub-limits, must be clearly told to the policyholder before renewal. Otherwise the insurer may be held to the earlier terms.
judgments.status_note: IRDAI's current product and policyholder rules also govern disclosure of changes at renewal.

judgments.title: Manmohan Nanda v. United India Assurance Co. Ltd
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud and B.V. Nagarathna JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a health insurer reject a claim by citing a medical condition that the insured disclosed, and that the insurer assessed, before issuing the policy?
holding: The insurer must assess the risks from the health condition disclosed in the proposal form before it issues the policy.
Once the policy is issued after that assessment, the insurer cannot reject a claim by citing a disclosed existing condition that led to the risk claimed for.
impact: Underwriting must be done before issue. A health insurer that conducted a medical examination and accepted disclosed conditions cannot later rely on them to repudiate.

judgments.title: GTL Infrastructure Ltd v. Canara Bank
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal Nos. 7449 and 7450 of 2021 and Writ Petition (C) No. 649 of 2021
judgments.bench: Uday Umesh Lalit and S. Ravindra Bhat JJ.
judgments.topic: Lenders cannot be forced into a majority deal
judgments.issue: Do RBI's rules on sale of loans to ARCs, or the inter-creditor agreement under the June 2019 framework, oblige a dissenting bank to follow the majority of lenders?
holding: No. Under paragraph 6.4 of RBI's Master Circular on prudential norms (IRAC) of 1 July 2015, on sale of financial assets to ARCs, each bank decides for itself whether to accept an offer; the 75% clause does not oblige a dissenting bank to sell.

The June 2019 framework did not stop Canara Bank from starting insolvency, and banks cannot be compelled to accept a borrower's settlement or resolution plan. The Bombay High Court's dismissal of the writ petitions was upheld.
impact: Borrowers cannot use RBI's stressed-asset rules to force a lender into a majority deal. The binding effect of the 75% decision is a matter between lenders who signed the inter-creditor agreement.
statutes: RBI Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, 7 June 2019, paras 9-10
RBI Master Circular on Prudential Norms on Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning, 1 July 2015, para 6.4

links.label: Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk (loan transfers, co-lending)
Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning
Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.status_note: RBI's stressed asset and loan transfer rules now sit in its consolidated Directions for each regulated entity.
judgments.facts: Most of GTL Infrastructure's lenders agreed to sell their loans to an asset reconstruction company, and the GTL group's domestic lenders signed an inter-creditor agreement under RBI's June 2019 stressed assets framework. Canara Bank did neither and filed for insolvency. The borrowers asked the courts to compel it to follow the majority.

judgments.title: KSE Electricals Pvt Ltd v. Project Director
judgments.bench: Moushumi Bhattacharya J.
judgments.topic: Stopping invocation of a bank guarantee
judgments.issue: When can a court stop a beneficiary from invoking an unconditional bank guarantee?
holding: Courts rarely interfere with bank guarantees, but an injunction is available in cases of fraud, irretrievable injustice or special equities, or where the invocation does not conform to the terms of the guarantee.
On the facts the invocation was not in terms of the guarantees and special equities existed, so the injunction was confirmed.
impact: Banks paying under guarantees should check that the demand matches the guarantee's terms exactly.
judgments.facts: A contractor asked the court to restrain the employer from invoking bank guarantees it had furnished, arguing the invocation did not follow the terms of the guarantees.

judgments.title: Ajoy Khanderia v. Barclays Bank
judgments.bench: Rajiv Sahai Endlaw and Asha Menon JJ.
judgments.topic: Pledgor's liability is limited to the pledge
judgments.issue: Is a third-party pledgor liable for the shortfall after the pledged goods are sold?
holding: No. Under section 176 of the Contract Act, the pawnee can sue the debtor for the shortfall, but a pledgor who is not the debtor or a guarantor is liable only up to the value of the pledged goods.
impact: Lenders who want recourse beyond the pledged assets must take a guarantee from the third-party pledgor.
judgments.facts: A person pledged securities to a bank for a loan to someone else but was neither the borrower nor a guarantor. After selling the pledged securities, the bank sought to recover the shortfall from him.

judgments.title: Franklin Templeton Trustee Services Pvt Ltd v. Amruta Garg (July 2021)
judgments.bench: S. Abdul Nazeer and Sanjiv Khanna JJ.
judgments.topic: Winding up: trustees and SEBI powers
judgments.issue: Can trustees wind up a scheme without unitholders' prior consent, and are Regulations 39 to 42 valid?
holding: Regulations 39 to 42 are valid. Being economic regulations, they get judicial restraint.
Read together with Regulation 18(15)(c), the trustees' opinion that the scheme should be wound up stands, but the consent of unitholders is a precondition for the winding up.
impact: Trustees cannot close a scheme on their own. They need unitholder consent, which shapes how stress in debt schemes is handled. Under regulation 36(5) of the 2026 Regulations, a scheme reopens for business if consent is not obtained.
judgments.status_note: Decided under the 1996 Regulations, which the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced from 1 April 2026. Regulations 36 to 38 of the 2026 Regulations carry the same consent requirement.

judgments.title: Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India
judgments.bench: L. Nageswara Rao and S. Ravindra Bhat JJ.
judgments.topic: Personal guarantors after a resolution plan
judgments.issue: Could the Government bring Part III of the Code into force only for personal guarantors to corporate debtors, and does approval of the company's resolution plan release the guarantor?
holding: The notification is valid. The Code itself treats personal guarantors to corporate debtors as a separate class, and bringing the provisions into force for that class alone is not excessive delegation.

Approval of a resolution plan for the corporate debtor does not by itself discharge the personal guarantor. A discharge of the principal borrower by operation of law, such as in insolvency, does not release the surety.
The National Company Law Tribunal dealing with the company's insolvency is also the forum for proceedings against its personal guarantor (section 60(2)).
impact: A lender can pursue the promoter's personal guarantee for the unpaid balance even after the borrower company's resolution plan is approved, and can start insolvency resolution against the guarantor before the NCLT.
Whether the guarantee survives still depends on its terms and on the plan: a plan may itself deal with guarantees.
judgments.status_note: From 26 May 2026 the interim moratorium on filing an application no longer applies to personal guarantors of corporate debtors (IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026).
judgments.facts: By a notification of 15 November 2019 the Central Government brought the personal insolvency provisions of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code into force only for personal guarantors to corporate debtors. Promoters and directors who had guaranteed company loans challenged the notification in several High Courts, and the cases were transferred to the Supreme Court.

judgments.title: India Resurgence ARC Pvt Ltd v. Amit Metaliks Ltd
judgments.bench: Vineet Saran and Dinesh Maheshwari JJ.
judgments.topic: Dissenting secured creditor's payout under a plan
judgments.issue: Can a dissenting secured financial creditor challenge an approved resolution plan on the ground that it gets less than the value of its security?
holding: No. How the plan money is shared among creditors is a matter for the commercial wisdom of the committee of creditors. A dissenting secured creditor cannot insist on being paid by reference to the value of its security.
What the Code assures a dissenting financial creditor is the minimum amount set out in section 30(2)(b). It cannot enforce its security interest outside the plan.
Courts review an approved plan only on the limited grounds in sections 30(2) and 61(3).
impact: A secured lender in the minority is bound by the majority's distribution. Its protection is the statutory minimum for dissenting creditors, so its vote and the negotiation inside the committee matter more than a later challenge.
judgments.status_note: The minimum payout was re-stated in 2026: under the new section 30(2)(ba), dissenting financial creditors must get at least the lower of their liquidation entitlement under section 53 and what they would get if the plan amount were distributed in the section 53 order. It does not apply where the plan was approved before 26 May 2026.
judgments.facts: An asset reconstruction company held security over the corporate debtor's assets which it valued far above what the resolution plan offered it. The plan was approved by about 95 per cent of the committee of creditors. The ARC voted against it and argued that the committee had to take the value of each creditor's security into account.

judgments.title: Shikha Nischal v. National Insurance Company Ltd
judgments.bench: Prathiba M. Singh J.
judgments.issue: Can a health insurer treat mental illness differently from physical illness?
holding: Section 21(4) of the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 requires every insurer to provide medical insurance for treatment of mental illness on the same basis as physical illness. Insurers are bound by the Act regardless of any circular.
The insurer was ordered to pay costs because the policyholder had to litigate. IRDAI was asked to ensure that all insurers give effect to section 21(4) from 29 May 2018, when it came into force.
impact: Health policies cannot exclude or sub-limit mental illness in a way that does not apply to physical illness. Claims for mental health treatment must be assessed on the same basis.

judgments.title: Technology Development Board v. Anil Goel
judgments.bench: Bansi Lal Bhat J. (Acting Chairperson), Ashok Kumar Mishra and Alok Srivastava
judgments.topic: Equal ranking of secured creditors in liquidation
judgments.issue: In liquidation, do secured creditors who give up their security keep their priority over particular assets?
holding: No. Secured creditors who relinquish their security to the liquidation estate all rank equally under section 53(1)(b)(ii), whatever their prior inter se priority.
impact: The Supreme Court stayed this ruling on 29 June 2021, and the question of inter se priority is pending before it. Lenders should keep priority arguments open and consider whether to realise security themselves under section 52.
judgments.status_note: Stayed by the Supreme Court on 29 June 2021; the appeal is pending.
judgments.facts: In a liquidation, a lender with a first charge on specific assets argued it should be paid from those assets before lenders with a second or no charge on them.

judgments.title: Indus Biotech Pvt Ltd v. Kotak India Venture (Offshore) Fund
judgments.case_no: Arbitration Petition (Civil) No. 48 of 2019 with connected matters
judgments.bench: S.A. Bobde CJI, A.S. Bopanna and V. Ramasubramanian JJ.
judgments.issue: When a section 7 application and a request to refer the dispute to arbitration are both pending, which comes first?
holding: The tribunal must first decide whether there is a default under section 7. If it admits the application, the proceedings become proceedings in rem and the dispute is no longer arbitrable.
If no default is found and the application is rejected, the parties can go to arbitration. On the facts there was no default, and the Court appointed an arbitral tribunal.
impact: An arbitration clause does not stop a lender from filing under section 7, but the tribunal will look at whether a default is really shown before admitting.
judgments.facts: An investor holding optionally convertible redeemable preference shares in Indus Biotech filed a section 7 application, claiming a default on redemption. Indus Biotech asked the tribunal to refer the dispute to arbitration under section 8 of the Arbitration Act.

judgments.title: Small Scale Industrial Manufactures Association v. Union of India
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan, R. Subhash Reddy and M.R. Shah JJ.
judgments.issue: Could courts order a full interest waiver, sector-wise relief or a longer moratorium during the COVID-19 pandemic?
holding: Economic and financial policy of RBI and the Government is open to only limited judicial review. Courts will not order particular relief packages, a full waiver of interest or a longer moratorium.
No interest on interest, compound interest or penal interest could be charged for the moratorium period. Any amount already recovered had to be refunded or adjusted in the next instalment.
impact: Lenders had to reverse interest on interest and penal interest for the moratorium period for all borrowers.
Courts will usually defer to RBI on the design of relief and restructuring schemes, unless they are arbitrary, mala fide or contrary to law.

links.label: Responsible Business Conduct (Fair Practices, KFS, penal charges, recovery)

judgments.title: Ayan Mallick v. State Bank of India
judgments.bench: Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya J.
judgments.topic: IBC moratorium does not stop wilful defaulter action
judgments.issue: Does the IBC moratorium on the company protect its directors and guarantors from wilful defaulter proceedings?
holding: No. The moratorium protects the corporate debtor and its assets. Wilful defaulter proceedings target the conduct of the persons behind the company and are not a recovery action against it.
For this purpose the corporate veil can be lifted to look at the conduct of directors and promoters.
impact: Lenders may run wilful defaulter proceedings against promoters, directors and guarantors while the borrower is in insolvency.
statutes: RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters

links.label: Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters

judgments.facts: A bank started proceedings to declare a company's directors and guarantors wilful defaulters while the company was under insolvency. The directors argued that the moratorium under section 14 of the IBC barred the bank from proceeding.

judgments.title: Amitabha Dasgupta v. United Bank of India
judgments.bench: Mohan M. Shantanagoudar and Vineet Saran JJ.
judgments.topic: Bank's duty of care for lockers
judgments.issue: What duty does a bank owe a locker holder, and can it be held liable under consumer law for breaking open a locker without notice?
holding: Breaking open the locker without notice and in breach of the Reserve Bank's instructions was a gross deficiency in service. The bank was directed to pay Rs 5 lakh as compensation and Rs 1 lakh as litigation costs.
Whatever the contract says, a bank cannot disclaim all responsibility for lockers. It owes a separate duty of care in running the facility.

The Court laid down interim rules: a locker register and key register, notice before any change in allotment, a record of access, breaking open only as the law permits and after notice, with an inventory, and no unilateral or unfair terms. The Reserve Bank was directed to issue comprehensive rules within six months.
A disputed claim about what was inside the locker needs evidence and goes to the civil court.
impact: The Reserve Bank's revised safe deposit locker instructions of August 2021, including the model locker agreement and the bank's liability where loss is due to its negligence or staff fraud, follow from this ruling.
Banks should be able to show notice, an inventory and a witnessed procedure before any locker is broken open.
judgments.facts: A bank broke open a customer's locker without notice, wrongly believing rent was unpaid, and allotted it to someone else. When the customer came to operate it, only some of the ornaments were returned. The consumer fora awarded modest compensation and left the dispute over the contents to a civil court.

judgments.title: Franklin Templeton Trustee Services Pvt Ltd v. Amruta Garg (February 2021)
judgments.bench: S. Abdul Nazeer and Sanjiv Khanna JJ.
judgments.issue: When trustees wind up a scheme, what does 'consent of the unitholders' under Regulation 18(15)(c) mean?
holding: Consent means consent of a majority of the unitholders who take part in the poll, not a majority of all unitholders of the scheme.
Consent of the majority binds all unitholders, including those who did not agree. The Court accepted the e-voting results for the six schemes.
impact: Trustees seeking unitholders' consent to wind up need a simple majority of those voting. Regulation 36(4) of the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 now writes this in: votes are counted at one vote per unit, and results must be published within 45 calendar days of the winding-up notice.
judgments.status_note: Decided under the 1996 Regulations, which the SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 2026 replaced from 1 April 2026. Regulation 36(4) of the 2026 Regulations reflects this ruling. Read with the July 2021 judgment in the same case.

judgments.title: Phoenix ARC Pvt Ltd v. Ketulbhai Ramubhai Patel
judgments.bench: Ashok Bhushan, R. Subhash Reddy and M.R. Shah JJ.
judgments.topic: A pledgor for another's loan is not a financial debtor
judgments.issue: Is a lender who holds a pledge from a company for a loan to a different borrower a financial creditor of the pledgor?
holding: No. The pledgor had no liability to repay the loan. Following Anuj Jain (Jaypee Infratech), security alone does not make the lender a financial creditor; at best it is a secured creditor of the pledgor.
impact: Where a group company provides security, lenders should also take a guarantee or make it a co-borrower so that they rank as financial creditors in its insolvency.
judgments.facts: A company had pledged shares it held in another company to secure a loan given to its parent. Phoenix ARC, as assignee of the loan, claimed in the pledgor's insolvency as a financial creditor.

judgments.title: Phoenix ARC Pvt Ltd v. Spade Financial Services Ltd
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud, Indu Malhotra and Indira Banerjee JJ.
judgments.topic: Collusive loans and related parties in the creditors' committee
judgments.issue: Are sham or collusive transactions 'financial debt', and can an entity that stopped being a related party before insolvency sit on the committee of creditors?
holding: A transaction that is sham or collusive is not a financial debt, even if it is dressed up as a loan. The money must have been disbursed against consideration for the time value of money in a real transaction.

The definition of 'related party' is wide. The bar in the first proviso to section 21(2) is normally tested at the time the committee is formed, but it also covers a creditor that ceased to be a related party only to get around the bar.
impact: Genuine lenders can challenge the admission of promoter-linked claims and their voting share. Resolution professionals should look at the substance of inter-corporate deposits and at recent changes in shareholding or directorships of claimants.

A lender that takes equity, board seats or other control rights in a borrower should check whether it risks being treated as a related party. The Code has a specific carve-out for regulated financial creditors that become related only through conversion of debt into equity.
judgments.facts: In the insolvency of a real estate company, two entities connected with its promoter group claimed to be financial creditors on the basis of inter-corporate deposits and a property development arrangement, and sought seats on the committee of creditors. An asset reconstruction company holding genuine debt objected that the transactions were collusive and that the claimants were related parties who had shed that status before the insolvency began.

judgments.title: Haryana Space Application Centre (HARSAC) v. Pan India Consultants Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: L. Nageswara Rao, Indu Malhotra and Ajay Rastogi JJ.
judgments.issue: Can an officer with a controlling influence over a party act as its arbitrator, and how is a tribunal whose mandate has lapsed replaced?
holding: The Principal Secretary had a controlling influence over the State agency, so he was ineligible under section 12(5) read with the Seventh Schedule.
With both parties' consent, the Court used its power under section 29A(6) to replace the tribunal with a retired Supreme Court judge as sole arbitrator, continuing from the stage reached.
impact: A senior officer of a party, or of a government controlling it, cannot sit as that party's arbitrator. Courts can replace a tribunal whose time has lapsed.
statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 29A, Seventh Schedule
judgments.facts: HARSAC, a nodal agency of the Haryana government, appointed the State's Principal Secretary as its nominee arbitrator in a dispute with a contractor. The tribunal's mandate later lapsed under section 29A and the contractor applied for a substitute tribunal.

judgments.title: Manish Kumar v. Union of India
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman, Navin Sinha and K.M. Joseph JJ.
judgments.topic: Minimum number of homebuyers to file
judgments.issue: Is the 2020 amendment requiring at least 100 allottees, or 10% of allottees, of the same project (whichever is less) to file an insolvency application valid?
holding: The threshold is valid. A critical mass of allottees of the same real estate project must agree before the Code is triggered.
Allottees are financial creditors, but they have features that set them apart from other financial creditors, such as their large numbers, which justify the separate threshold.
impact: An individual homebuyer can no longer push a developer into insolvency unless the threshold is met, which in a small project may need only a few allottees. Housing finance lenders to developers face fewer stray insolvency filings, though collective filings remain possible.
statutes: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Amendment) Act, 2020, s. 3

judgments.title: Volkswagen Finance Pvt Ltd v. Shree Balaji Printopack Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: A.I.S. Cheema J. and Shreesha Merla
judgments.topic: Unregistered vehicle loan charge in liquidation
judgments.issue: Is a vehicle financier with an endorsement on the registration certificate, but no registered charge, a secured creditor in liquidation?
holding: No. Without registration under section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 or any other proof required by the Liquidation Regulations, the financier could not be treated as a secured creditor. An endorsement under the Motor Vehicles Act is not enough.
impact: Vehicle and equipment lenders to companies must register the charge with the Registrar of Companies and CERSAI, not rely only on the RC endorsement. Compare Home Kraft (2025) on the CIRP stage.

links.label: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.facts: An NBFC had financed a car for a company. Its hypothecation was endorsed on the vehicle's registration certificate but not registered as a charge with the Registrar of Companies, an information utility or CERSAI. In the company's liquidation it claimed as a secured creditor.

judgments.title: Magma Fincorp Ltd v. Rajesh Kumar Tiwari
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud and Indira Banerjee JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a financier repossess a vehicle under a hire purchase agreement without notice, and what relief can a consumer forum give if it does?
holding: Under a hire purchase agreement the financier remains the owner until all instalments are paid, and may take back the vehicle on default as the agreement provides.

Whether notice is needed before repossession depends on the terms of the agreement, express or implied. If the agreement requires notice, repossessing without it is a breach and a deficiency in service.

The remedy for such a breach is damages for the loss actually caused. A refund of all instalments, which were in substance hire charges for use of the vehicle, is not automatic. On the facts there was no deficiency.
impact: NBFCs financing vehicles should follow the notice terms of their own agreements and the Reserve Bank's fair practices code, and take possession peacefully. A repossession that follows the contract will not be treated as deficient service only because the borrower objects.

links.label: Registration, Exemptions and Scale Based Regulation

judgments.facts: A borrower took a vehicle on hire purchase from an NBFC and paid 7 of 35 instalments. The financier repossessed and sold the vehicle. The consumer fora held that repossession without notice was a deficiency in service and ordered a refund of the instalments paid, with compensation.

judgments.title: Srikanth Dwarakanath (Liquidator of Surana Power Ltd) v. Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd
judgments.bench: Venugopal M. J., V.P. Singh and Shreesha Merla
judgments.issue: Can a secured creditor with a shared charge enforce its security outside liquidation on its own?
holding: No. Read with section 13(9) of SARFAESI, a secured creditor with a non-exclusive charge needs the agreement of creditors holding at least 60% in value of the debt secured on the same assets before it can realise them under section 52.
impact: Consortium lenders with pari passu security must coordinate before opting out of the liquidation estate.

links.label: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.facts: A secured creditor with a pari passu charge over assets of a company in liquidation sought to realise its security outside the liquidation, although it did not hold 60% of the secured debt on those assets.

judgments.title: Amitabh Kumar Jha v. Bank of India
judgments.bench: Bansi Lal Bhat J., Venugopal M. J. and V.P. Singh
judgments.topic: Inter-creditor agreement does not stop one lender filing
judgments.issue: Does an inter-creditor agreement prevent one consortium lender from filing for insolvency on its own?
holding: No. The agreement governed relations among the lenders and expressly preserved each lender's rights against the borrower. The borrower had no standing to rely on it.
The appeal was dismissed as frivolous.
impact: Borrowers cannot rely on lenders' inter-creditor arrangements to resist insolvency by one lender. The Supreme Court took the same view in GTL Infrastructure (2021).
statutes: RBI Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets, 2019
judgments.facts: Bank of India, one of a consortium of lenders to a toll-road company, filed under section 7 after a default of about Rs 21.68 crore. A director argued that the inter-creditor agreement among the lenders barred a single lender from acting alone.

judgments.title: Transcon Skycity Pvt Ltd v. ICICI Bank Ltd
judgments.bench: G.S. Patel J.
judgments.issue: Should the 90-day NPA period run while the national lockdown was in force?
holding: As an interim measure, the lockdown period was excluded from the 90-day period for NPA classification, without deciding the merits.
The court said expressly that the order was not a precedent.
impact: The order was overtaken by RBI's COVID-19 moratorium circulars and the Supreme Court's ruling in Small Scale Industrial Manufacturers Association (2021).
statutes: RBI Prudential Norms on Income Recognition and Asset Classification

links.label: Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning

judgments.status_note: Interim, expressly not a precedent, and overtaken by the Supreme Court's 2021 ruling on the COVID-19 moratorium.
judgments.facts: A borrower whose instalments were overdue before March 2020 asked the court to stop its lender from classifying the account as an NPA during the COVID-19 lockdown.
