judgments.title: Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman, Aniruddha Bose and V. Ramasubramanian JJ.
judgments.issue: Could RBI direct the entities it regulates to stop serving anyone dealing in virtual currencies?
holding: The RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act and the Payment and Settlement Systems Act together give RBI very wide powers over the currency, credit and payment systems, enough to cover virtual currency activity that may affect them.

However, the circular of 6 April 2018 failed the test of proportionality, because RBI had not found that virtual currency exchanges had actually harmed the entities it regulates. The circular was set aside.
impact: RBI's directions to regulated entities are tested for proportionality as well as for power. A blanket ban needs evidence of harm and a look at less drastic options.
The judgment confirms how wide RBI's statutory powers are, including the NBFC powers in Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act.

judgments.title: Anuj Jain, Interim Resolution Professional for Jaypee Infratech Ltd v. Axis Bank Ltd
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal Nos. 8512-8527 of 2019 with connected matters
judgments.bench: A.M. Khanwilkar, Ajay Rastogi and Dinesh Maheshwari JJ.
judgments.topic: Mortgages for a parent's loans: preferential and not financial debt
judgments.issue: Were the mortgages preferential transactions, and are lenders holding only such third-party security financial creditors of the company that gave it?
holding: The mortgages were preferential transactions under section 43: they were given to benefit a related party (the parent), within the two-year look-back for related parties, and not in the ordinary course of business. They were set aside.
A lender who holds only a mortgage from a company for someone else's loan, with no claim against that company to repay, is not its financial creditor. At most it is a secured creditor.
impact: Third-party security from group companies is vulnerable in their insolvency. Lenders who want a vote and a claim should take a guarantee as well as the security.
judgments.facts: Jaypee Infratech had mortgaged its land to secure loans that banks gave to its parent, Jaiprakash Associates. In Jaypee Infratech's insolvency, the resolution professional asked for these mortgages to be set aside as preferential, and the parent's lenders claimed to be financial creditors of Jaypee Infratech.

judgments.title: Canara Bank v. United India Insurance Co Ltd
judgments.bench: S. Abdul Nazeer and Deepak Gupta JJ.
judgments.topic: Insurance of hypothecated goods: bank's and insurer's duties
judgments.issue: Can persons for whose benefit a policy is taken claim under it as consumers, and what is the position of the bank that required the insurance?
holding: A beneficiary of a policy is a consumer even though he is not a party to it. The farmers could claim directly against the insurer.
An insurer relying on an exclusion must prove it. Where the fire was not caused by the insured, the reason for the fire does not defeat the claim.

A bank that insists on insurance of hypothecated goods and is in touch with the insurer has a duty to see that the cover is in place and the insurer is informed. Because of its own deficiency the bank could recover only simple interest at 12 per cent a year and not the contractual rate.
impact: Lenders that require borrowers to insure the security should track that the policy is issued, names the right interests and is renewed. A lapse can cost the lender its contractual interest.
judgments.facts: Farmers stored their produce in a cold store and took bank loans against it. The cold store had taken a fire policy covering the stock, at the bank's insistence. A fire destroyed the stock. The insurer rejected the claim, alleging that the fire was not accidental and that the farmers were strangers to the policy; the bank kept charging interest on the loans.

judgments.title: Perkins Eastman Architects DPC v. HSCC (India) Ltd
judgments.bench: Uday Umesh Lalit and Indu Malhotra JJ.
judgments.topic: A party cannot appoint the sole arbitrator
judgments.issue: Can a person who has an interest in the dispute appoint the sole arbitrator, even if he is not himself the arbitrator?
holding: No. A person who is ineligible to act as arbitrator because of interest cannot appoint a sole arbitrator either. Whoever has an interest in the outcome will have an element of exclusivity in choosing the arbitrator.
The Court appointed an independent sole arbitrator.
impact: Unilateral appointment clauses in loan and other contracts cannot be relied on. The Constitution Bench in CORE (2024) confirmed the principle.
judgments.status_note: Confirmed by the Constitution Bench in Central Organisation for Railway Electrification v. ECI SPIC SMO MCML (2024), whose ruling on unilateral appointment applies to appointments made after 8 November 2024.
judgments.facts: The contract allowed the chairman and managing director of HSCC, a public sector company, to appoint the sole arbitrator. A dispute arose and the foreign contractor asked the Supreme Court to appoint an independent arbitrator.

judgments.title: Jignesh Shah v. Union of India
judgments.case_no: Writ Petition (Civil) No. 455 of 2019 with connected matters
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman, R. Subhash Reddy and Surya Kant JJ.
judgments.topic: Limitation for winding-up and insolvency petitions
judgments.issue: When does the limitation period start for a winding-up or insolvency petition based on a debt?
holding: Article 137 of the Limitation Act applies: the petition must be filed within three years from the date of default.
Filing a suit for the debt does not extend that period for a winding-up or insolvency petition. The two remedies are separate.
The petition, filed more than three years after the default, was time-barred and could not continue.
impact: Lenders must start insolvency within three years of default, unless the debt is acknowledged in writing (which restarts limitation) or another exclusion applies.
judgments.facts: IL&FS Financial Services filed a winding-up petition against La-Fin Financial Services in October 2016 on a debt that had fallen due in August 2012. The petition was transferred to the NCLT and treated as an insolvency application.

judgments.title: Authorised Officer, Indian Bank v. D. Visalakshi
judgments.bench: A.M. Khanwilkar and Dinesh Maheshwari JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a Chief Judicial Magistrate deal with a secured creditor's request under section 14 of SARFAESI to take possession?
holding: Yes. In non-metropolitan areas the Chief Judicial Magistrate is competent, as the expressions CMM and CJM are interchangeable. This settled conflicting High Court views.
The power under section 14 is non-judicial: it is the State's coercive power to help the secured creditor take possession.
impact: Lenders outside metropolitan areas can apply to the CJM as well as the District Magistrate under section 14, which helps when the DM is slow to act.

links.label: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.title: Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd v. Union of India
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman, Sanjiv Khanna and Surya Kant JJ.
judgments.issue: Is the 2018 amendment to the IBC that treats allottees of real estate projects as financial creditors constitutional?
holding: The amendment is valid. Allottees are financial creditors who can start insolvency under section 7 and sit on the Committee of Creditors through authorised representatives.
RERA must be read harmoniously with the Code. Where the two conflict, the Code prevails.
impact: In a builder's insolvency, homebuyers can hold a large share of the votes in the Committee of Creditors. This can dilute the voting power of lenders to builders, including HFCs and NBFCs, depending on the amounts admitted for each class.
Construction finance needs to price the risk that homebuyers will drive the resolution plan.
judgments.status_note: See also Manish Kumar (2021) on the minimum number of allottees.

judgments.title: State Bank of India v. Jah Developers Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Vineet Saran JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a borrower be represented by a lawyer before a lender's committees that decide wilful default?
holding: The in-house committees under RBI's wilful defaulter circular exercise administrative, not judicial, power. A borrower has no right to be represented by a lawyer before them.

Being declared a wilful defaulter directly affects the right to carry on business under Article 19(1)(g). The First Committee's order must be given to the borrower, who can represent to the Review Committee within 15 days, and the Review Committee must pass a reasoned order that is served on the borrower.
impact: Wilful default classification needs a show-cause notice, a chance to reply, a reasoned order and review. Under the judgment, lawyers can be kept out of the in-house proceedings.

RBI's Wilful Defaulter Directions of 2024 now go further: the Review Committee must also give the borrower, guarantor, promoter or director an opportunity for a personal hearing. Follow the Directions for the current procedure.
statutes: RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 2015

links.label: Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters

judgments.title: Cooperatieve Rabobank U.A. v. Shailendra Ajmera (Ruchi Soya Industries)
judgments.bench: S.J. Mukhopadhaya J. (Chairperson) and Bansi Lal Bhat J.
judgments.topic: Discounting a supplier's bills makes the bank an operational creditor
judgments.issue: Is a bank that discounted a supplier's bills a financial creditor of the buyer?
holding: No. The bank stood in the shoes of the supplier and its claim arose from the supply of goods. It was an operational creditor of the buyer.
impact: Banks discounting receivables without recourse to the buyer's own borrowing should expect to rank as operational creditors in the buyer's insolvency.
judgments.facts: A foreign supplier sold goods to Ruchi Soya and Rabobank discounted the supplier's bills of exchange drawn on Ruchi Soya. In Ruchi Soya's insolvency Rabobank claimed as a financial creditor.

judgments.title: Reliance Life Insurance Co. Ltd v. Rekhaben Nareshbhai Rathod
judgments.bench: D.Y. Chandrachud and Hemant Gupta JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a life insurer repudiate because the insured did not disclose another life policy taken shortly before?
holding: Insurance contracts rest on utmost good faith. The duty of full disclosure means no information of substance or interest to the insurer may be omitted or concealed.
The insured had answered 'no' when asked about existing cover, two months after taking another policy. The repudiation was within the period allowed by section 45 and was upheld.
impact: Questions on existing cover in the proposal form are material. Insurers can rely on wrong answers to them, within the time allowed by section 45.

Section 45 was amended in 2015: a life policy now cannot be questioned on any ground after three years from the date of issue, commencement of risk, revival or rider, whichever is later. Within three years, the insurer must still show the grounds section 45 requires and communicate them in writing.
judgments.status_note: Decided under section 45 as it stood before the 2015 amendment.

judgments.title: Bharat Broadband Network Ltd v. United Telecoms Ltd
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Vineet Saran JJ.
judgments.issue: Is an arbitrator appointed by a person who is ineligible under section 12(5) also ineligible, and can the parties waive this by conduct?
holding: A person ineligible under section 12(5) and the Seventh Schedule cannot appoint another arbitrator. The appointment was void and the arbitrator's mandate terminated.
Ineligibility can be waived only by an express agreement in writing made after the dispute arose. Taking part in the arbitration or filing a statement of claim is not a waiver.
impact: Loan agreements that let the lender's officer appoint the sole arbitrator are vulnerable. The Constitution Bench in CORE (2024) and Bhadra (2026) built on this line.
statutes: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, ss. 12(5), 14, 15, Seventh Schedule
judgments.facts: The chairman and managing director of a public sector company appointed the sole arbitrator under the contract. After the TRF ruling of 2017, the company itself sought to remove the arbitrator, arguing he was ineligible.

judgments.title: Dharani Sugars and Chemicals Ltd v. Union of India
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Vineet Saran JJ.
judgments.issue: Was RBI's circular of 12 February 2018 on resolution of stressed assets (the 'one-day default' framework) within its powers?
holding: Sections 35AA and 35AB of the Banking Regulation Act are valid. They confer regulatory powers on RBI and are not manifestly arbitrary.

RBI can direct banks to start insolvency under the IBC only under section 35AA, and only for specific defaults by specific debtors, with Central Government authorisation. A direction aimed at debtors generally is outside section 35AA.

The circular also relied on section 45L of the RBI Act for NBFCs, but nothing showed that section 45L(3) was satisfied. Because banks and NBFCs could not be separated, the circular was declared ultra vires as a whole.
impact: RBI's power to push lenders into insolvency is case-specific. A general framework cannot be used to compel lenders to start insolvency, though lenders can still choose the IBC themselves as part of a resolution.
For NBFCs, directions under section 45L must meet that section's conditions. The current stressed-asset rules for NBFCs were issued on this footing.
judgments.status_note: RBI later replaced the struck-down circular with a new prudential framework.

judgments.title: Deputy Director, Directorate of Enforcement v. Axis Bank
judgments.case_no: Criminal Appeal No. 143 of 2018 with connected appeals
judgments.bench: R.K. Gauba J.
judgments.topic: PMLA attachment versus a secured lender
judgments.issue: Can the ED attach property already mortgaged to a bona fide lender, and whose claim prevails?
holding: The ED can attach 'property of equivalent value' even if it is not tainted, but the attachment does not defeat a prior charge of a bona fide secured creditor who had no part in the offence.

Where the secured creditor had begun enforcement (under SARFAESI, the RDB Act or the IBC) before the attachment, the attachment is subject to its charge and may only reach any value above the secured debt.
The appeals were sent back to the Appellate Tribunal to apply these principles.
impact: Lenders facing a PMLA attachment should show that the mortgage predates the offence, that they acted in good faith, and when enforcement began. Section 32A of the IBC and the IBBI's 2025 circular on restitution of PMLA-attached assets now help in insolvency cases.

links.label: Restitution of assets attached under PMLA

judgments.facts: The Enforcement Directorate attached properties under the Prevention of Money-laundering Act that had been mortgaged to banks before the alleged offence. The Appellate Tribunal had released the properties in favour of the banks.

judgments.title: Vijay Kumar Jain v. Standard Chartered Bank
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal No. 8430 of 2018 with Writ Petition (Civil) No. 1266 of 2018
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Navin Sinha JJ.
judgments.issue: Are members of the suspended board entitled to see the resolution plans considered by the committee of creditors?
holding: Members of the suspended board may attend committee meetings under section 24(3), and to take part meaningfully they must be given the resolution plans.
The resolution professional may ask them for a confidentiality undertaking before sharing the plans.
The Court directed the committee to consider the plans afresh with the directors participating.
impact: Lenders and resolution professionals should circulate plans to suspended directors with a confidentiality undertaking. A plan approved without this can be challenged.
judgments.facts: A former director of a company in insolvency asked for copies of the resolution plans placed before the committee of creditors. The resolution professional refused and the appellate tribunal upheld the refusal.

judgments.title: Swiss Ribbons Pvt Ltd v. Union of India
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Navin Sinha JJ.
judgments.issue: Is the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code constitutional, in particular its different treatment of financial and operational creditors?
holding: The Code is constitutionally valid.

Financial creditors are different from operational creditors: they are best placed to assess the viability of the corporate debtor and the resolution plan. Giving only them a vote in the Committee of Creditors is not discriminatory.
A financial creditor must prove a 'default', while an operational creditor only claims a debt. The different triggers in sections 7 and 9 are therefore justified.
impact: Financial creditors, including NBFCs and HFCs, vote in the Committee of Creditors and so have a strong say in the outcome. Section 7 is a route to collective resolution of a defaulting company, not a debt collection tool, though lenders often recover through it.

judgments.title: Pushpa Shah v. IL&FS Financial Services Ltd
judgments.bench: S.J. Mukhopadhaya J. (Chairperson) and Bansi Lal Bhat J.
judgments.topic: Put option obligations as financial debt
judgments.issue: Is an obligation to buy back shares at a price that gives the investor a return a financial debt?
holding: Yes. The transaction had the commercial effect of a borrowing, because the amount was raised against the time value of money. It fell within section 5(8)(f), so the investor was a financial creditor.
impact: Structured equity with a guaranteed exit can be a financial debt. In the related appeal, Jignesh Shah v. Union of India (2019), the Supreme Court held a winding-up petition on the same debt time-barred, without disturbing this point.
judgments.facts: An NBFC bought shares in a group company under an arrangement that obliged a group entity to buy them back at a price giving the NBFC a return. When the buy-back was not honoured, the NBFC filed under section 7.

judgments.title: Vishnu Kumar Agarwal v. Piramal Enterprises Ltd
judgments.bench: S.J. Mukhopadhaya J. (Chairperson) and Bansi Lal Bhat J.
judgments.issue: Can a financial creditor start a second insolvency for the same debt against another guarantor?
holding: The tribunal held that once a claim was admitted in one corporate debtor's insolvency, a second application for the same debt against another corporate debtor was not maintainable, though the creditor could file against both at once.
impact: The Supreme Court later held in Maitreya Doshi (2022) that insolvency can run against both co-obligors, subject to no double recovery. The NCLAT's restriction is no longer followed.
judgments.status_note: Not followed: the NCLAT itself departed from it in later cases, and the Supreme Court allowed parallel proceedings in Maitreya Doshi (2022) and BRS Ventures (2024).
judgments.facts: A lender had already admitted its claim in the insolvency of one corporate guarantor and then filed a second section 7 application against another corporate guarantor for the same debt.

judgments.title: Binani Industries Ltd v. Bank of Baroda
judgments.case_no: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 82 of 2018 with connected appeals
judgments.bench: S.J. Mukhopadhaya J. (Chairperson) and Bansi Lal Bhat J.
judgments.topic: Maximising value and treating creditors fairly
judgments.issue: What is the purpose of the resolution process, and can a plan discriminate between creditors of the same kind?
holding: The objective of the IBC is resolution and maximisation of the value of assets, not recovery for particular creditors.
A plan that discriminates among similarly placed creditors without reason is not in line with the IBC. The tribunal set aside the earlier plan and approved the higher, non-discriminatory plan.
impact: Lenders on a committee should be able to justify differences in treatment between creditors. The Supreme Court later held in Essar Steel (2019) that different treatment of secured and unsecured creditors is permitted if it is fair.
judgments.status_note: Read with the Supreme Court's ruling in Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel v. Satish Kumar Gupta (2019).
judgments.facts: In Binani Cement's insolvency the committee of creditors approved a plan that treated some financial and operational creditors less favourably than others. A rival bidder then offered a higher plan that paid creditors more fairly.

judgments.title: ArcelorMittal India Pvt Ltd v. Satish Kumar Gupta
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Indu Malhotra JJ.
judgments.issue: How is section 29A applied to resolution applicants, and what are the roles of the committee of creditors and the tribunals?
holding: Section 29A is read by looking at the substance: 'control', 'management' and 'connected person' cover persons who act jointly or in concert, and the corporate veil may be lifted to see who really stands behind a bid.
Both bidders were ineligible when they bid, but were given a chance to become eligible by paying the overdue debts of the connected defaulting companies within two weeks.
The feasibility and commercial merits of a plan are for the committee of creditors. The tribunals review only legality. Time lost in litigation may be excluded from the CIRP timeline.
impact: Lenders on a committee of creditors must test eligibility under section 29A on substance and cannot leave it to the resolution professional alone.
judgments.facts: In the insolvency of Essar Steel, the resolution professional found both bidders, ArcelorMittal and Numetal, ineligible under section 29A: ArcelorMittal because of its link to a defaulting company, Numetal because of its link to the Ruia promoters.

judgments.title: K. Kishan v. Vijay Nirman Company Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Indu Malhotra JJ.
judgments.topic: Arbitral award under challenge is a dispute
judgments.issue: Can an operational creditor start insolvency on an arbitral award that is under challenge?
holding: A pending challenge under section 34 means there is a pre-existing dispute, so the section 9 application cannot be admitted.
The IBC is not a tool to recover debts or to pressure a debtor into paying an award it is lawfully contesting.
impact: A creditor with an award that is under challenge should enforce it through execution once the challenge fails, not through the IBC.
judgments.facts: A contractor obtained arbitral awards against a company and then served an IBC demand notice and filed a section 9 application for the awarded sums. The company had already challenged the awards under section 34 of the Arbitration Act.

judgments.title: ITC Ltd v. Blue Coast Hotels Ltd
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal Nos. 2928-2930 of 2018 with connected appeals
judgments.bench: S.A. Bobde and L. Nageswara Rao JJ.
judgments.topic: SARFAESI sale and a borrower's conduct
judgments.issue: Can a borrower who has repeatedly sought time and not paid have a SARFAESI sale set aside on procedural grounds?
holding: The secured creditor was entitled to take possession and sell. On the law as it then stood, the borrower's right to redeem the property ended when the sale was made.
A borrower whose conduct was to seek time repeatedly without paying cannot rely on non-compliance with section 13(3A), and is not entitled to discretionary relief under Article 226.
impact: Courts look at the borrower's conduct before granting writ relief against a SARFAESI sale. A sale can still be set aside for failure to follow section 13 and the Security Interest Rules. Since the 2016 amendment to section 13(8), the right to redeem ends on publication of the sale notice (Celir LLP, 2023).

links.label: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.status_note: The right of redemption after the 2016 amendment to section 13(8) is now explained in Celir LLP (2023).
judgments.facts: IFCI took action under SARFAESI against a hotel company in Goa and sold the hotel to ITC. The borrower had repeatedly sought time and promised to pay. The High Court set the sale aside for defects in the SARFAESI procedure, including the response to the borrower's objection under section 13(3A).

judgments.title: State Bank of India v. SKC Retails Ltd
judgments.bench: S.J. Mukhopadhaya J. (Chairperson) and Bansi Lal Bhat J.
judgments.topic: Who pays the interim resolution professional
judgments.issue: Who must bear the interim resolution professional's fees and expenses?
holding: Under Regulation 33 of the CIRP Regulations, the applicant who filed the petition and proposed the interim resolution professional bears the expenses first.
The committee of creditors reimburses the applicant to the extent it ratifies the expenses, which then form part of the insolvency resolution process costs.
impact: A lender that files should budget for the interim professional's fees and seek ratification at the first committee meeting.
statutes: IBBI (Insolvency Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, reg. 33
judgments.facts: The NCLT directed the committee of creditors to bear the interim resolution professional's expenses in proportion to their claims. SBI, a committee member, appealed.

judgments.title: United India Insurance Co Ltd v. Jai Parkash Tayal
judgments.bench: Prathiba M. Singh J.
judgments.issue: Is a blanket exclusion of 'genetic disorders' in a health insurance policy valid?
holding: A broad exclusion of all genetic disorders is too wide, ambiguous and discriminatory. It violates Article 14, and it is contrary to public policy when used to deny claims.
The right to avail of health insurance is part of the right to health and healthcare under Article 21.
The insurance regulator was asked to look again at exclusion clauses so that claims are not rejected on the basis of genetic disorders. The decree for Rs 5 lakh with interest was upheld.
impact: Health insurers cannot rely on a general 'genetic disorder' exclusion. The regulator afterwards told insurers not to reject claims on that basis and standardised the permitted exclusions.
Exclusions added at renewal without clear notice to the policyholder are open to challenge.
judgments.status_note: The insurer's special leave petition, filed in 2018, is pending in the Supreme Court.
judgments.facts: A policyholder with a heart condition (hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy) was refused a mediclaim payout under an exclusion for 'genetic disorders' that the insurer had added to the policy at a renewal. The trial court decreed his suit, and the insurer appealed.

judgments.title: SEBI v. Rakhi Trading Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: Kurian Joseph and R. Banumathi JJ.
judgments.issue: Can pre-arranged, reversed trades in the futures and options segment be manipulative, even though they are cash-settled?
holding: Yes. Trading is meant to make profit. Where one party consistently loses in pre-planned, rapid reversal trades, the trades are not genuine and amount to an unfair trade practice.
The Securities Appellate Tribunal was wrong to hold that such trades in the F&O segment cannot manipulate the market because there is no change of beneficial ownership.
SEBI's appeals against the brokers were dismissed. Merely facilitating a trade is not a violation, and SEBI had shown no negligence or connivance by the brokers.
impact: Clients who trade in pre-arranged reversals in derivatives are exposed to action even though the trades are cash-settled. A broker is liable only on proof of its own negligence or connivance, so surveillance alerts and records of client instructions matter.

judgments.title: Mobilox Innovations Pvt Ltd v. Kirusa Software Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Sanjay Kishan Kaul JJ.
judgments.issue: When does a dispute raised by the debtor defeat an operational creditor's insolvency application?
holding: If the debtor shows a plausible dispute about the debt that existed before the demand notice, the tribunal must reject the section 9 application. The dispute need not already be in a suit or arbitration.
The tribunal does not decide who is right. It only separates a real dispute that needs further investigation from one that is spurious, hypothetical or patently feeble.
impact: Suppliers, service providers and other operational creditors cannot use the IBC to recover disputed dues. Financial creditors under section 7 are not subject to this test.
judgments.facts: Kirusa, which provided tele-voting services, sent Mobilox a demand notice for unpaid invoices and applied under section 9 of the IBC. Mobilox replied that Kirusa had breached a non-disclosure agreement, so the amounts were disputed.

judgments.title: SEBI v. Kanaiyalal Baldevbhai Patel
judgments.bench: Ranjan Gogoi and N.V. Ramana JJ.
judgments.issue: Can front-running by persons who are not intermediaries be punished under the PFUTP Regulations?
holding: Information about trades a large investor is about to place is that investor's confidential information.

A person who passes on such information in breach of duty, and a 'tippee' who knows of the breach and trades on it, can both be liable for fraud under Regulations 3 and 4(1) of the PFUTP Regulations. Non-intermediary front-running is covered.
impact: Fund managers, dealers and anyone with advance knowledge of a fund's orders, and those they tip off, are exposed to SEBI action. AMCs need controls on order information and on staff and related-party trading.
statutes: SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to Securities Market) Regulations, 2003, regs. 3, 4(1)

judgments.title: Innoventive Industries Ltd v. ICICI Bank
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Sanjay Kishan Kaul JJ.
judgments.topic: Admission of a creditor's insolvency petition
judgments.issue: What must the tribunal examine before admitting a financial creditor's application, and can a State relief law suspending a company's debts block insolvency under the IBC?
holding: On a section 7 application the tribunal only has to be satisfied that a default has occurred, that is, that a financial debt was due and has not been paid. The debtor may show that the debt is not due or not payable in law, but the creditor need not prove more.

The Maharashtra Act is repugnant to the IBC, a later Parliamentary law on the same subject, and gives way to it under Article 254 of the Constitution. A State law suspending liabilities cannot stop an IBC process.
The IBC is a complete code designed for speed; the tribunal must decide admission within the statutory timelines.
impact: Lenders filing under section 7 need clear proof of the debt and the default (loan documents, statements, record from an information utility). Arguments about the borrower's general hardship or other relief schemes do not defeat admission.
Later rulings refined the discretion to admit, but default remains the trigger for a financial creditor's petition.
judgments.facts: ICICI Bank applied under section 7 of the IBC to start insolvency against Innoventive Industries. The company argued that its liabilities stood suspended by a Maharashtra government notification under the Maharashtra Relief Undertakings (Special Provisions) Act, 1958, so no debt was payable.

judgments.title: Alka Chandewar v. Shamshul Ishrar Khan
judgments.bench: R.F. Nariman and Sanjay Kishan Kaul JJ.
judgments.topic: Enforcing an arbitral tribunal's interim orders
judgments.issue: Can disobedience of an arbitral tribunal's interim order be punished as contempt?
holding: Yes. Under section 27(5), a person who fails to comply with an arbitral tribunal's interim order is guilty of contempt of the tribunal, and the tribunal may make a representation to the court, which can punish as for contempt of court.
From 23 October 2015 section 17(2) also makes the tribunal's interim orders enforceable as if they were orders of the court.
impact: Lenders that get interim relief from an arbitral tribunal (for example, to secure a vehicle or deposit funds) can enforce it through the court.
judgments.facts: A party ignored interim orders made by an arbitral tribunal under section 17 of the Arbitration Act. The tribunal referred the default to the court under section 27(5), but the Bombay High Court held that it had no power to punish for such disobedience.

judgments.title: Starlog Enterprises Ltd v. ICICI Bank Ltd
judgments.bench: S.J. Mukhopadhaya J. (Chairperson) and Balvinder Singh
judgments.issue: Can a section 7 application be admitted without notice to the company?
holding: The admission was set aside. The company must be given notice and a hearing before admission, and the claim and default must be properly shown.
Costs were imposed on the bank.
impact: Lenders must serve the application and get the figures right; defective filings delay the process and can attract costs.
judgments.facts: The NCLT admitted ICICI Bank's section 7 application against Starlog Enterprises ex parte. The company had not been served, and the claim did not match the record.

judgments.title: Sree Metaliks Ltd v. Union of India
judgments.bench: Debangsu Basak J.
judgments.issue: Is section 7 valid, and must the tribunal hear the company before admitting a financial creditor's application?
holding: Section 7 is valid. The tribunal must follow natural justice, which section 424 of the Companies Act makes it apply, so the company must be given notice and a chance to be heard before admission.
impact: Lenders filing under section 7 must serve the application on the company. Admission without notice can be set aside (see Starlog Enterprises).
judgments.facts: A company against which a bank had filed a section 7 application challenged the validity of section 7, arguing it did not give the company a hearing before admission.

judgments.title: IDFC Bank Ltd v. Ruchi Soya Industries Ltd
judgments.bench: R.D. Dhanuka J.
judgments.topic: Lone lender's winding-up petition while JLF restructures
judgments.issue: Should a winding-up petition by a small lender be admitted while the joint lenders' forum is pursuing revival?
holding: The petition was dismissed. Winding up is discretionary, and the court considered the wishes of the overwhelming majority of lenders who were pursuing revival under RBI's framework.
impact: Winding up has since been replaced by the IBC for insolvency, where any financial creditor may file on default. Ruchi Soya itself went through the IBC later.
statutes: RBI Framework for Revitalising Distressed Assets, 2014
judgments.status_note: Insolvency petitions are now under the IBC, where a lender's right to file does not depend on the majority's wishes.
judgments.facts: IDFC Bank, holding about 1% of Ruchi Soya's debt, filed a winding-up petition. The other lenders, holding about 98% of the debt, were working on a revival plan through a joint lenders' forum under RBI's framework.

judgments.title: SEBI v. Kishore R. Ajmera
judgments.bench: Ranjan Gogoi and Prafulla C. Pant JJ.
judgments.issue: What proof does SEBI need to hold a broker or sub-broker liable for manipulative trading?
holding: Direct proof of a meeting of minds is rarely available. Civil liability under the SEBI Act and its regulations is decided on the preponderance of probabilities; prosecution needs proof beyond reasonable doubt.
Liability can be inferred from circumstances such as the volume of trades, how long trading in a scrip persisted, the details of buy and sell orders and how close in time they were.
impact: Brokers can be penalised on circumstantial evidence for trades placed for clients, especially in illiquid scrips. Know-your-client checks, surveillance alerts and records of client instructions are the broker's main defence.

judgments.title: LIC of India v. Insure Policy Plus Services Pvt Ltd
judgments.bench: Vikramajit Sen and Shiva Kirti Singh JJ.
judgments.issue: Could an insurer refuse to register assignments of life policies made for trading?
holding: Under section 38 as it then stood, life policies were transferable and assignable. Once the procedure was followed, the insurer had to register the assignment, and its circular refusing assignments for trading was ultra vires.
The Court noted that section 38 as amended by the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015 now gives the insurer discretion whether to accept a transfer or assignment.
impact: Today an insurer may decline to act on an assignment where it has sufficient reason to believe the assignment is not bona fide, not in the policyholder's interest or in public interest, or is for trading in policies. It must record its reasons in writing before refusing (section 38(2) and (3)).
judgments.status_note: Section 38 was substituted by the Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act, 2015.

judgments.title: Reserve Bank of India v. Jayantilal N. Mistry
judgments.bench: M.Y. Eqbal and C. Nagappan JJ.
judgments.issue: Can RBI refuse to disclose inspection reports and other information about the entities it regulates under the Right to Information Act?
holding: RBI does not hold such information in a fiduciary relationship with the banks it regulates, and cannot refuse disclosure on the grounds of economic interest or commercial confidence in this case.
Inspection reports and similar documents obtained by RBI from a regulated entity are 'information' under section 2(f) of the RTI Act. RBI's duty is to the public, not to the regulated entity.
impact: Findings in RBI inspection reports can become public through RTI requests, subject to the exemptions in section 8 that apply on the facts. Regulated entities should expect supervisory findings to be disclosable.
judgments.status_note: In HDFC Bank Ltd v. Union of India (30 September 2022, 2022 INSC 1056) the Supreme Court held that banks' writ petitions questioning this judgment are maintainable, observing that prima facie it did not balance the right to information against the right to privacy.

judgments.title: Tata Capital Financial Services Ltd v. Unity Infraprojects Ltd
judgments.case_no: Arbitration Petition No. 800 of 2014 and Company Petition No. 443 of 2014
judgments.bench: G.S. Patel J.
judgments.issue: Can an NBFC outside a CDR package wind up the borrower or seize its assets while the banks' restructuring is under way?
holding: The court refused to admit the winding-up petition while the CDR package was in progress.
The receiver and the injunction were vacated. The NBFC was allowed to join the CDR, and otherwise had to be told before any disposal of assets.
impact: Under the IBC a lender that has not joined a restructuring can still file on default, and RBI's framework now binds only lenders who sign the inter-creditor agreement.
judgments.status_note: Winding up for inability to pay debts has been replaced by the IBC.
judgments.facts: An NBFC had given a term loan of about Rs 50 crore to a construction company. When the company defaulted, its banks put it into corporate debt restructuring (CDR), which the NBFC had not joined. The NBFC sought interim relief, a receiver and winding up.

judgments.title: Stock Exchange, Bombay v. V.S. Kandalgaonkar
judgments.bench: R.M. Lodha CJI, Kurian Joseph and R.F. Nariman JJ.
judgments.topic: Exchange's lien over a defaulting broker
judgments.issue: When a broker defaults, who gets paid first from the membership card and the deposited securities: the stock exchange or the Income Tax Department?
holding: A membership card is only a personal privilege granted by the exchange under its rules. Its sale proceeds cannot be paid over to the Income Tax Department for the member's tax dues.
For securities deposited with the exchange, the exchange's lien makes it a secured creditor with priority over Government dues.
impact: Securities a broker has deposited with the exchange are first applied to the broker's obligations under the exchange's rules, ahead of tax dues. The membership card's value is not available to the tax department.

judgments.title: Ionic Metalliks v. Union of India
judgments.case_no: Special Civil Application No. 645 of 2014 with No. 10120 of 2014
judgments.bench: Akil Kureshi and J.B. Pardiwala JJ.
judgments.topic: Wilful defaulter rules and independent directors
judgments.issue: Is RBI's wilful defaulter regime valid, and can it be applied to every director of a defaulting company?
holding: The Master Circular is valid, including the bar on fresh credit and the five-year bar on new ventures. It has statutory backing under the Banking Regulation Act.

Treating every director as a wilful defaulter regardless of role is arbitrary. Only directors shown to be responsible may be named, and promoter-directors are treated differently. A show-cause notice must give particulars of the alleged wilful default.
A private bank is not amenable to the writ jurisdiction, so the petition against it was not maintainable.
impact: Lenders must identify the specific role of each director before naming them. RBI's current wilful defaulter directions build in these safeguards: non-whole-time directors are named only where their involvement is shown.
statutes: RBI Master Circular on Wilful Defaulters, 2 July 2012

links.label: Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters

judgments.status_note: The 2012 Master Circular has been replaced by RBI's Master Direction on Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters, 2024, which includes these safeguards.
judgments.facts: Two borrowers and their directors challenged RBI's Master Circular on wilful defaulters of 2 July 2012 and show-cause notices issued to them by banks. One petition was against a private sector bank.

judgments.title: Yes Bank Ltd v. A2Z Maintenance & Engineering Services Ltd
judgments.bench: Manmohan Singh J.
judgments.issue: Can a lender with an exclusive charge be made to share its security under a restructuring it did not join?
holding: No. A CDR package binds only lenders who are party to it. Yes Bank was entitled to protect its exclusive charge, and the borrower was restrained from dealing with the charged assets.
impact: Lenders that do not sign an inter-creditor agreement are not bound by the majority's decisions, but the resolution plan must give dissenting lenders at least their liquidation value.
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIX
judgments.status_note: CDR has been replaced by RBI's June 2019 framework, under which lenders holding 75% by value and 60% by number bind those who sign the inter-creditor agreement.
judgments.facts: Yes Bank held an exclusive charge over certain assets of a borrower. The borrower went into corporate debt restructuring, which Yes Bank did not join, and the CDR package proposed sharing that security with the other lenders.

judgments.title: Citicorp Maruti Finance Ltd v. S. Vijayalaxmi
judgments.bench: Altamas Kabir, Cyriac Joseph and Surinder Singh Nijjar JJ.
judgments.issue: Can a financier take back a vehicle by force under a hire-purchase agreement?
holding: Even for goods under hire-purchase, recovery must follow the law. The owner-financier cannot use force to take back possession on the strength of the agreement.
RBI's guidelines support this. Recovery in breach of those guidelines, or of the principles laid down by the Supreme Court, will be struck down.
impact: Vehicle and asset financiers must repossess through lawful process, with no force or intimidation. Recovery agents act for the lender, and the lender answers for them.
Consumer forums can award compensation for unlawful repossession.
statutes: RBI Fair Practices Code and recovery guidelines

links.label: Responsible Business Conduct (Fair Practices, KFS, penal charges, recovery)

judgments.title: BNY Corporate Trustee Services Ltd v. Wockhardt Ltd
judgments.bench: S.C. Dharmadhikari J.
judgments.issue: Can a bond trustee petition for winding up on non-payment of matured bonds while the company is under restructuring with its other lenders?
holding: The trustee had standing and the debt was due and unpaid, so the petition was admitted. Corporate debt restructuring with banks did not bind bondholders who were not part of it.
impact: The same principle now applies under the IBC: a debenture trustee may file for insolvency on behalf of bondholders, and a lender-only restructuring does not bind holders who did not join.
judgments.status_note: Insolvency petitions are now under the IBC.
judgments.facts: Wockhardt failed to redeem foreign currency convertible bonds on maturity. The bond trustee filed a winding-up petition. Wockhardt argued that it was under corporate debt restructuring and that the trustee lacked standing.

judgments.title: Transcore v. Union of India
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal No. 3228 of 2006 with connected matters
judgments.bench: Arijit Pasayat and S.H. Kapadia JJ.
judgments.issue: Must a bank withdraw its DRT application before using SARFAESI, and is symbolic possession of immovable property valid?
holding: SARFAESI remedies are in addition to the DRT remedy. The doctrine of election does not apply, and the bank need not withdraw its DRT application first.

Under Rule 8 of the Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, possession of immovable property under section 13(4) may be symbolic; the bank may then seek physical possession through the Magistrate under section 14.
impact: Lenders can pursue DRT recovery and SARFAESI enforcement in parallel, as long as they do not recover twice.
statutes: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993, s. 19

links.label: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act

judgments.facts: Banks with recovery applications pending before the Debts Recovery Tribunal started SARFAESI action against the same borrowers without withdrawing those applications. The borrowers argued that the banks had to elect one remedy and that symbolic possession was not enough.

judgments.title: Kerala State Financial Enterprises Ltd v. Official Liquidator, High Court of Kerala
judgments.bench: S.B. Sinha and Dalveer Bhandari JJ.
judgments.topic: Unregistered charge and attachment in winding up
judgments.issue: Does a lender with an unregistered charge, or with an attachment under a revenue recovery law, rank as a secured creditor in a winding up?
holding: A charge not registered under section 125 of the Companies Act, 1956 is void against the liquidator and creditors.
An attachment does not create a charge. A government company's dues are not government dues, so the lender was an unsecured creditor and the Companies Act prevailed.
impact: Registering every charge with the Registrar (now section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013) remains essential. See the NCLAT's rulings in Volkswagen Finance and Home Kraft for how this plays out under the IBC.
judgments.status_note: Decided under the Companies Act, 1956; the registration rule is now in section 77 of the 2013 Act.
judgments.facts: A government-owned chit company lent to a company and attached its properties under the Kerala Revenue Recovery Act. Its charge was never registered with the Registrar of Companies. When the borrower was wound up, the chit company asked for leave to continue the sale.

judgments.title: ICICI Bank Ltd v. SIDCO Leathers Ltd
judgments.bench: S.B. Sinha and P.K. Balasubramanyan JJ.
judgments.topic: First and second charge holders in liquidation
judgments.issue: In a winding up, does a first charge holder keep its priority over a second charge holder?
holding: Yes. Section 529A puts workmen's dues and secured creditors' dues on an equal footing, but it does not abolish the priority among secured creditors that comes from section 48 of the Transfer of Property Act and their contracts.
impact: Lenders rely on this principle when arguing that charge priority should be respected in an IBC liquidation. The IBC's section 53 treats secured creditors who relinquish security as one class, and the NCLAT's rulings on pro-rata distribution (see Technology Development Board and later cases) are being tested in the Supreme Court.
judgments.status_note: Decided under the Companies Act, 1956. Under the IBC, priority among secured creditors in liquidation is pending in the Supreme Court.
judgments.facts: ICICI Bank held a first charge over a company's assets and another lender held a second charge. When the company was wound up, the second charge holder argued that section 529A of the Companies Act, which ranks secured creditors pari passu with workmen, also wiped out priority among secured creditors.

judgments.title: Indian Bank v. Official Liquidator, Chemmeens Exports (P) Ltd
judgments.case_no: Civil Appeal arising from M.C.A. No. 11 of 1986 (Kerala High Court)
judgments.bench: B.N. Kirpal and Syed Shah Mohammed Quadri JJ.
judgments.topic: Unregistered mortgage merged in a decree
judgments.issue: Is a mortgage decree void against the liquidator because the underlying charge was not registered?
holding: It depends on the decree. If the decree keeps the unregistered charge alive, section 125 applies and it is void against the liquidator. If the time to pay under the decree has passed and what operates is an order for sale, the matter has passed from contract to judgment and the decree stands.
On the facts the time to pay had expired before the liquidator applied, so the decree was valid.
impact: A decree may protect a lender whose charge was not registered, but registration is the only safe course.
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Order XXXIV
judgments.status_note: Decided under the Companies Act, 1956.
judgments.facts: Indian Bank obtained a mortgage decree (giving time to pay before sale) against a company. The mortgage had not been registered with the Registrar of Companies. When the company was wound up, the official liquidator asked the court to declare the decree void.
